objectives.objective: Define emergency medical services (EMS) systems.
objectives.summary: EMS is a coordinated system that provides emergency care and transport, rather than a single ambulance crew.

sections.heading: How the system works
paragraphs: EMTs, paramedics, dispatchers, hospital personnel, and other responders work together to reach sick or injured people, provide prehospital care, and move patients to the next level of treatment. State laws govern the system. Individual services must operate within those laws and their medical direction.
bullets: Public access begins with a request for help, commonly through 9-1-1. Dispatchers obtain information, send resources, and may give emergency instructions.
Field assessment, treatment, packaging, and transport are connected to hospital care through an effective handoff.
Medical direction, education, equipment, information systems, quality improvement, and administration support the people providing care.
Continuity of care means treatment proceeds as a coordinated process from the scene through the receiving facility.

sources.locator: EMS system definition and team roles

objectives.objective: Name the four levels of EMT training and licensure.
objectives.summary: The four levels, from the most basic to the most advanced, are EMR, EMT, AEMT, and paramedic.

sections.heading: Know each name
paragraphs: These are provider training and licensure levels. They describe increasing preparation and skills; the exact authority to perform those skills is controlled by state law and local medical direction.
bullets: Emergency Medical Responder (EMR): immediate basic care before the ambulance arrives, followed by assistance to the arriving crew.
Emergency Medical Technician (EMT): basic emergency assessment, treatment, and transport.
Advanced Emergency Medical Technician (AEMT): EMT care plus selected advanced life support skills.
Paramedic: extensive advanced life support assessment and treatment.
Do not substitute nurse or physician in this four-level sequence. Those are other health professions, although they may work within the EMS system.

objectives.objective: Describe EMT licensure criteria; include how the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) applies to employment as an EMT.
objectives.summary: Completing an EMT course is one step toward certification and state licensure; it does not by itself authorize practice.

sections.heading: General criteria
bullets: High school diploma or equivalent, required immunizations, a background check and drug screening, and a valid driver’s license.
A recognized health care provider BLS/CPR course and a state-approved EMT course.
Required state-recognized written and practical certification examinations.
Mental and physical ability to safely perform the EMT role, plus applicable state, local, and employer requirements.

sections.heading: Certification, licensure, and disability
paragraphs: Certification examinations establish that required knowledge and skills have been demonstrated. State licensure is the state process that permits an individual to function as a health care provider. Requirements vary by jurisdiction.

The ADA protects access to government programs and services and equal employment opportunity for people with disabilities. Title I protects applicants with disabilities and may require changes to the work environment or the way tasks are performed. The central task requirement remains safe performance of the EMT role; a disability alone is not a reason to assume a person cannot perform it.

objectives.objective: Discuss the historic background of the development of the EMS system.
objectives.summary: Modern EMS developed from military field care, organized ambulance services, and later efforts to improve civilian emergency care.

sections.heading: Development in order
bullets: World War I: volunteer ambulances. World War II: field care. Korean conflict: field medics and rapid helicopter evacuation.
1966: Accidental Death and Disability: The Neglected Disease of Modern Society, often called the White Paper, drew attention to inadequate emergency care and is a major origin point for modern EMS.
Early 1970s: DOT published an EMT curriculum. In 1971, the first EMT textbook was published by the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons.
1973: the Emergency Medical Services Act supplied funding and development programs.
Late 1970s: a recommended National Standard Curriculum supported more consistent education. During the 1980s, additional advanced provider training expanded ALS care.
1990s: the EMS Agenda for the Future described a plan for EMS development and standardization. In 2019, EMS Agenda 2050 revised the long-term vision.

sources.locator: History of EMS; Overview of the EMS System

objectives.objective: Describe the levels of EMT training in terms of skill sets needed for each of the following: EMR, EMT, AEMT, and paramedic.
objectives.summary: Provider levels differ in preparation and authorized skills, but basic assessment and patient safety remain important at every level.

sections.heading: Skill sets
bullets: EMR: immediate BLS and urgent care with limited equipment, often provided by firefighters or law enforcement before an ambulance arrives. EMRs continue assisting EMTs afterward.
EMT: patient assessment, basic emergency care, packaging, and transport. Examples include CPR/AED use, bleeding control, airway adjuncts, and assistance with certain medications.
AEMT: additional selected ALS skills, including IV therapy, advanced airway adjuncts, and a limited number of emergency medications.
Paramedic: a broad range of ALS skills, including endotracheal intubation, emergency pharmacology, cardiac monitoring, and advanced assessment and treatment.

sections.heading: Authority to perform a skill
paragraphs: The National EMS Scope of Practice Model provides overarching skill guidance. State laws regulate provider operations, and the local medical director supplies daily oversight and protocols. Learning about a skill does not independently authorize its use.

sources.locator: Emergency Medical Responder; Emergency Medical Technicians; AEMT; Paramedic

objectives.objective: Recognize the possible presence of other first responders at a scene with EMR training, some knowledge of first aid, or merely good intentions, and their need for direction.
objectives.summary: People already helping at a scene may have very different training. The EMT must assess their capabilities and give clear direction.

sections.heading: Use available help safely
paragraphs: An EMR may be a police officer or firefighter trained to begin immediate BLS while waiting for the ambulance. Other people may know CPR or first aid. Some bystanders may have no medical training but want to help. The presence of a uniform or willingness to assist does not establish a particular skill level.

On arrival, the EMT assumes responsibility for assessment, care, packaging, and transport. Gather information about what has happened and what care has already been given. Direct helpers to appropriate tasks rather than assuming they know the next step.
bullets: EMRs can continue assisting after the EMT arrives.
Give instructions that fit the helper’s actual training and the resources available.
Coordinate tasks and maintain scene safety for responders, the patient, and bystanders.

objectives.objective: Explain the guiding principles of EMS Agenda 2050.
objectives.summary: EMS Agenda 2050 is presented as a vision for a people-centered EMS system.

sections.heading: The vision described in class
paragraphs: The focus is on care organized around the person’s needs, with coordination across services rather than isolated encounters. The supplied material emphasizes both treatment and prevention.
bullets: Comprehensive, high-quality, convenient care.
Clinical care supported by evidence.
Efficient, well-rounded care.
Preventive care as well as emergency treatment.
Comprehensive patient records that are easily accessible to support care.
A work environment that attracts talented people and allows them to build rewarding EMS careers.

sections.heading: How this connects to practice
paragraphs: People-centered care requires information to follow the patient, cooperation among health services, and decisions that support patient outcomes. The EMT contributes through assessment, documentation, patient advocacy, and continuity of care.

objectives.gap: The supplied material describes the people-centered vision but does not enumerate all six named EMS Agenda 2050 guiding principles.

sections.heading: The six guiding principles
bullets: Inherently safe and effective: design care and operations to protect patients, clinicians, and the public, and use evidence to improve outcomes.
Integrated and seamless: coordinate EMS with health care, public health, public safety, and community services so care follows the person across settings.
Reliable and prepared: make dependable care available and prepare the system for routine demands and extraordinary events.
Socially equitable: give people access to appropriate care regardless of their background, resources, or location.
Sustainable and efficient: use funding, personnel, equipment, and time responsibly so the system remains available over the long term.
Adaptable and innovative: learn from results and adjust to changing community needs, evidence, and useful technology.

objectives.objective: Describe how medical direction of an EMS system works and the EMT’s role in the process.
objectives.summary: Medical direction provides the physician oversight and authorization under which EMTs deliver field care.

sections.heading: Two forms of direction
bullets: Off-line or indirect medical control: written protocols and standing orders, education, supervision, and other oversight provided without a live physician conversation.
Online or direct medical control: physician instructions given by telephone or radio during a patient encounter.

sections.heading: The EMT’s role
paragraphs: The medical director connects the service with the medical community and hospitals. Protocols describe the EMT’s authorized care, and standing orders identify what to do for particular complaints or conditions. Standing orders can be carried out without first contacting medical control each time.

The EMT must know and follow those protocols, recognize when online direction is needed, communicate useful patient information, and carry out authorized care. Medical direction does not replace state regulation: service practices must still comply with state laws, rules, and guidelines.

objectives.objective: Define mobile integrated healthcare and community paramedicine.
objectives.summary: Mobile integrated health care brings coordinated health services into the community; community paramedicine is one part of that approach.

sections.heading: Mobile integrated health care
paragraphs: MIH uses the prehospital health care system to improve access to affordable care. An integrated team of health professionals provides services in the community rather than requiring every encounter to occur in a physician’s office or hospital. The aim is to connect patients with care that meets their needs.

sections.heading: Community paramedicine
paragraphs: Experienced paramedics receive additional advanced training to provide community services beyond their usual emergency role. This is a specific expanded preparation, not an automatic duty of every EMT or paramedic.
bullets: Health evaluations.
Monitoring chronic illnesses and other ongoing conditions.
Obtaining laboratory samples.
Administering immunizations.

sections.heading: Distinction
paragraphs: MIH describes the broader method of delivering coordinated community care. Community paramedicine describes one trained provider role within it.

objectives.objective: Explain the purpose of the EMS continuous quality improvement (CQI) process.
objectives.summary: CQI reviews how the EMS system performs, identifies problems, and checks whether changes improve care.

sections.heading: The improvement process
paragraphs: Continuous quality improvement uses reviews and audits to find opportunities to improve and determine where remedial training is needed. The goal is to minimize errors and improve patient safety, not simply to count mistakes.
The plan–do–study–act cycle means planning a change, putting it into practice, examining the result, and then acting on what was learned. The process continues rather than ending after one review.

sections.heading: What supports it
bullets: Accurate patient care documentation provides information that can be reviewed.
The medical director maintains quality control.
Patient safety requires participation by both the organization and its personnel.
Errors may involve a rule, missing knowledge, a skill, or a combination.
A Just Culture balances fairness with accountability for behavioral choices and encourages learning. Remedial action should respond to the actual problem identified.

sources.locator: Evaluation; Continuous Quality Improvement; Patient Safety

objectives.objective: Characterize the EMT’s role in disease and injury prevention and public education in the community.
objectives.summary: The EMT supports public health by helping prevent illness and injury and teaching the community how to respond safely.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary prevention
paragraphs: Public health considers the needs of entire populations. EMS can work with public health agencies to reduce hazards before injuries occur and reduce harm when events do occur.
bullets: Primary prevention aims to keep an event from happening. Examples include education on pool safety and avoiding dangerous behaviors that cause crashes.
Secondary prevention reduces the effects of an event. The course places helmets and seat belts in this category because they reduce injury when a crash occurs.
Classify the purpose of the measure: preventing the event itself versus limiting injury from the event. A safety item can be used before an incident yet still serve injury reduction.

sections.heading: Community role
paragraphs: EMTs can participate in safety education and community CPR/first aid instruction, support public awareness of AEDs, and sustain helpful community relationships. Prevention complements emergency response rather than replacing it.

sources.locator: VII.N; Teaching Tips: CPR/first aid and AED awareness; VIII.B.17

objectives.objective: Describe the roles and responsibilities of the EMT.
objectives.summary: The EMT’s responsibilities extend from preparation before a call to safe care, transport, handoff, documentation, and ongoing professional development.

sections.heading: Before and during a call
bullets: Keep the vehicle and equipment ready. Operate the emergency vehicle safely.
Protect yourself, your partner, the patient, and bystanders. Evaluate the scene and obtain additional resources when needed.
Act as an on-scene leader, gain access to the patient, assess the patient, and provide appropriate emergency care.
Provide emotional support to the patient, family, and other responders.

sections.heading: Completing care and supporting the system
bullets: Coordinate with other health professionals to maintain continuity of care.
Resolve the incident while meeting medical and legal standards. Protect confidentiality and patient privacy.
Complete administrative responsibilities, including documentation and necessary service information.
Continue professional development as knowledge and skills change.
Build community relationships and contribute to the profession.

sections.heading: Professional obligation
paragraphs: These responsibilities apply to paid and volunteer EMTs. Both are health care professionals and are expected to provide competent, respectful care.

sources.locator: Roles and Responsibilities of the EMT; Integration of Health Services

objectives.objective: Describe the attributes an EMT is expected to possess.
objectives.summary: Professional attributes make the EMT reliable, safe, respectful, and effective as a member of a care team.

sections.heading: Attributes and their meaning
bullets: Integrity: be fair and honest. Empathy: recognize and consider another person’s needs.
Self-motivation: identify and solve problems without waiting to be directed.
Appearance and hygiene: present yourself in a way that supports confidence and trust.
Self-confidence: know both your abilities and limitations, and ask for help when needed.
Time management: perform or delegate multiple tasks efficiently without sacrificing safety.
Communication: understand others and make your own meaning clear.
Teamwork and diplomacy: recognize your team role and communicate respectfully.
Respect: treat other people as important. Patient advocacy: keep the patient’s needs central.
Careful delivery of care: attend to details and perform care as safely as possible.

sections.heading: Apply them consistently
paragraphs: Every patient deserves compassion, respect, and the best care you can provide, including patients who are upset or do not treat you respectfully. Professional conduct depends on your responsibilities, not on how agreeable the patient is.

sources.locator: Roles and Responsibilities of the EMT

objectives.objective: Explain the impact of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) on patient privacy.
objectives.summary: HIPAA draws attention to protecting patient information, and EMTs are bound by patient confidentiality.

sections.heading: What to protect
paragraphs: Information learned during care includes the patient’s history, findings from assessment, treatment, and private disclosures. Respecting privacy allows patients to share information needed for care without expecting it to become public conversation.

Share findings with those treating the patient. The material also recognizes limited disclosures required by law to police or social service agencies. The existence of an emergency does not make all information public.

sections.heading: Practical distinction
bullets: A clinical handoff supports continuing treatment and is an appropriate purpose for sharing relevant information.
An unrelated conversation about a recognizable patient does not support treatment.
Protect privacy while assessing and treating the person, and protect the information recorded afterward.

sections.heading: Connection to professionalism
paragraphs: Patient advocacy and careful care include protecting dignity and confidentiality. HIPAA supports that obligation; it is not a reason to omit the information the receiving care team needs.

sources.locator: Roles and Responsibilities of the EMT: privacy

objectives.objective: Explain the steps that contribute to wellness and resilience and their importance in managing stress.
objectives.summary: Wellness is the active pursuit of health; resilience is the ability to cope with distress and recover from it.

sections.heading: Build a daily foundation
bullets: Eat balanced meals, maintain hydration, and use complex carbohydrates for sustained energy.
Aim for 7–9 hours of sleep a day. Include movement, stretching, and exercise; the course describes at least 30 minutes of moderate or vigorous activity on 5 days each week.
Maintain supportive family, friend, and colleague relationships. Develop interests outside EMS.
Practice mindfulness and a positive outlook. Take time off and vacations rather than relying on constant overtime.

sections.heading: Manage the stressor
paragraphs: Reduce avoidable stress, adjust work hours or the work environment when possible, and talk with people you trust. Seek professional counseling when needed. Focus on care you can provide rather than repeatedly dwelling on circumstances you cannot change.
Eustress is a helpful stress response that can improve focus and energy. Distress is a harmful response. Good habits and support help prevent distress from accumulating into exhaustion.

sources.locator: Wellness, resilience, and strategies to manage stress

objectives.objective: Differentiate infectious disease and communicable disease.
objectives.summary: An infectious disease is caused by harmful organisms; a communicable disease can spread between people or species.

sections.heading: Know the distinction
paragraphs: Infectious describes the cause of illness: organisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi, or parasites enter or affect the body. Communicable describes the ability of an illness to spread from one host to another. These terms answer different questions: what causes it, and can it be transmitted?

A pathogen is a microorganism capable of causing disease in a susceptible person. Contamination means pathogens or foreign material are present on or in an object, wound, or body. Exposure means contact occurred in a way that could permit transmission. Exposure does not automatically establish infection.

sections.heading: Why it matters for EMS
paragraphs: Protective techniques, immunization, and hand hygiene reduce risk. Do not wait for a patient to have a confirmed communicable diagnosis before using standard precautions. The patient’s appearance alone does not tell you whether organisms can be transmitted.

objectives.objective: Identify the risks and hazards of sleep deprivation in EMS.
objectives.summary: Sleep deprivation threatens safe decisions, driving, physical performance, and long-term health.

sections.heading: Risks
paragraphs: Short-term fatigue contributes to medical errors, vehicle crashes, and harm to patients, bystanders, and EMS personnel. Long-term sleep deprivation is associated in the course with hypertension, sleep apnea, respiratory problems, diabetes, depression, and other conditions. Stress and poor sleep can worsen one another.

sections.heading: Reduce fatigue
bullets: Aim for 7–9 hours of good-quality sleep. The course fatigue-management guidance favors shifts shorter than 24 hours and opportunities to nap.
Where permitted, a 20–30 minute nap or rest break during a shift can help. Physical and mental activity can support alertness.
Use caffeine thoughtfully; avoid caffeine and nicotine for at least 4 hours before sleep.
Keep the sleep area dark, quiet, and cool. Maintain a consistent schedule and a calming presleep routine.
Avoid heavy meals immediately before sleep, exercise earlier, and balance fluid intake. Fatigue monitoring and education are organizational responsibilities too.

objectives.objective: State the routes of disease transmission.
objectives.summary: Transmission is the route through which an infectious agent moves from its source to another person.

sections.heading: Five routes
bullets: Direct contact: contact with infected blood or other body fluids. Bloodborne exposures are a major EMS example.
Indirect contact: contact through a contaminated object, including a used needle or inadequately cleaned equipment.
Airborne transmission: inhalation of infectious particles from the respiratory tract; coughing or sneezing can spread them.
Foodborne transmission: ingestion of contaminated food or water.
Vector-borne transmission: a carrier such as a flea, tick, or mosquito transmits the infection.

sections.heading: Connect the route to protection
paragraphs: Gloves and careful sharps handling limit contact exposure. Eye and face protection address splashes. Appropriate respiratory protection addresses inhaled organisms. Cleaning equipment and hand hygiene limit transfer from contaminated surfaces.
A contaminated object is a potential source, while an exposure is the event that could allow transmission. Understanding that difference helps identify what happened and what follow-up is needed.

objectives.objective: Describe the specific routes of transmission and the steps to prevent and/or deal with an exposure to hepatitis, tuberculosis, or human immunodeficiency (HIV)/acquired immunodeficiency disorder (AIDS).
objectives.summary: Match protection to the transmission route: bloodborne exposure for HIV and hepatitis in this material, and inhalation risk for tuberculosis.

sections.heading: Prevent exposure
bullets: HIV and hepatitis: avoid contact with blood and body fluids. Wear gloves and add eye/face protection and a gown when splashes are likely.
Prevent needlesticks: do not recap, bend, or break needles. Put used sharps directly into an approved closed, rigid container.
Tuberculosis: use a fit-tested particulate respirator such as an N95. Place a surgical mask on the patient when appropriate to reduce spread.
Maintain required immunization records, including hepatitis B, and follow the department’s infection control plan.

sections.heading: If exposure occurs
paragraphs: Transfer patient care, clean exposed skin, rinse exposed eyes for 20 minutes, report the event, and obtain evaluation. The course describes antiviral treatment after significant HIV exposure, hepatitis B antibody evaluation and immune globulin when indicated, and evaluation/treatment after a positive TB test. These are follow-up decisions through the exposure-management process.

sources.locator: Masks, Respirators, and Barrier Devices; Sharps; Postexposure Management

objectives.gap: The sources do not provide hepatitis subtype-by-subtype transmission details or a complete disease-specific exposure medication schedule.

sections.heading: Transmission: distinguish the pathogens
bullets: Hepatitis A (HAV): primarily fecal–oral spread—infected stool contaminates hands, food, or water that reaches another person’s mouth. Handwashing and vaccination prevent infection; it is not primarily a bloodborne infection.
Hepatitis B (HBV): infectious blood or body fluids enter through a needlestick, mucous membrane, or broken skin. Vaccination and documented vaccine response are important occupational protection.
Hepatitis C (HCV): principally exposure to infected blood, especially a percutaneous injury. There is no vaccine.
HIV: occupational risk involves potentially infectious blood or fluid contacting a puncture wound, mucous membrane, or nonintact skin. Standard Precautions and safer sharps handling reduce exposure.

Tuberculosis: inhalation of airborne particles from a person with infectious pulmonary or laryngeal TB. Inactive/latent TB infection does not spread to others. Respiratory protection addresses this airborne route.

sections.heading: Exposure follow-up
bullets: HIV: report immediately and obtain urgent medical evaluation. PEP should begin as soon as possible and within 72 hours when indicated. A clinician selects the regimen; do not wait for symptoms.

HBV: evaluation uses both the source patient’s infection status and your documented vaccination/antibody response. A documented vaccine responder generally needs no HBV prophylaxis. Susceptible or inadequately protected personnel may need vaccine and/or hepatitis B immune globulin.
HCV: baseline testing and follow-up are used to identify infection. CDC does not recommend preventive HCV medication after occupational exposure; confirmed infection is referred for treatment.

TB: receive symptom screening. Previously negative personnel are tested when the exposure is identified and again 8–10 weeks after the last exposure. Personnel with documented prior positive tests receive symptom screening rather than another infection test.
HAV: when a relevant exposure has occurred, contact a clinician promptly; vaccination within two weeks may prevent illness, and immune globulin may be indicated based on age and health.

sources.title: CDC: Clinical Overview of Viral Hepatitis

outside.note: This supplement distinguishes hepatitis subtypes; the class section uses broader bloodborne shorthand. Your exposure-management clinician determines the actual treatment and follow-up schedule.

objectives.objective: Apply the standard precautions used in treating patients to prevent infection.
objectives.summary: Use standard precautions with every patient, because infectious risk may be present without visible symptoms.

sections.heading: During care
bullets: Perform hand hygiene before and after patient contact, including after wearing gloves.
Wear gloves when blood or body fluid contact is possible. Change gloves between patients.
Use goggles or a face shield for splashes; ordinary prescription glasses are insufficient. Add a gown when extensive contamination is likely.
Choose masks and respirators according to the exposure hazard. Put on and remove PPE in a consistent sequence to avoid contaminating yourself.
Avoid handling contaminated sharps unnecessarily; use the correct sharps container.

sections.heading: After care
paragraphs: Clean the ambulance after runs and routinely each day. Bag contaminated linen and medical waste appropriately. Clean and sterilize reusable equipment according to department procedures. Use heavy-duty utility gloves for cleaning.

Standard precautions protect providers and patients. Gloves do not replace handwashing, and a diagnosis is not needed before precautions begin. Report any potential exposure to the designated officer.

sources.locator: Risk Reduction and Prevention; PPE; Infection Control Routine

objectives.objective: Explain the steps to take for personal protection from airborne and bloodborne pathogens.
objectives.summary: Personal protection must prevent blood/body fluid contact and address inhaled pathogens when the scene presents that risk.

sections.heading: Bloodborne protection
bullets: Wear gloves and use eye/face protection when splashes are possible. A gown adds protection during extensive blood or body fluid exposure.
Use heavy-duty gloves for cleaning and dispose of sharps without recapping, bending, or breaking them.
Wash hands even when gloves were worn. Carefully remove contaminated PPE.

sections.heading: Airborne protection
paragraphs: Use a properly fitted and fit-tested particulate respirator, such as an N95, when airborne disease is suspected. A surgical mask on the patient provides source control when appropriate. Protective eyewear is also needed. A surgical mask used for fluid spatter is not the same equipment as a particulate respirator.

If oxygen is required, provide it with the appropriate oxygen device rather than allowing a source-control mask to interfere with necessary treatment. The course describes a nonrebreathing mask at 10–15 L/min in this context. Follow the department infection-control plan and report exposures.

objectives.objective: Demonstrate proper handwashing techniques.
objectives.summary: Wash before and after patient contact, even when you wore gloves, and scrub with soap for at least 20 seconds.

sections.heading: Hand hygiene sequence
bullets: Use soap and running water when available. Work up a lather and rub all surfaces of the hands for at least 20 seconds.
Pay particular attention to the fingernails, between fingers, and the backs of the hands.
Do not treat gloves as a substitute: small tears or contamination during removal can expose the hands.
If running water is unavailable, use a waterless handwashing substitute, then wash with soap and water when you reach a sink.

sections.heading: Waterless backup
paragraphs: The narration specifies an alcohol-based sanitizer containing at least 60% alcohol. Rub it across all hand surfaces, including between fingers and near the nails, until dry; do not wipe it off early.
Make hand hygiene part of every encounter rather than an occasional response to obvious contamination. This is identified as a simple and highly effective way to control transmission.

objectives.objective: Explain the ways in which immunity to infectious diseases is acquired.
objectives.summary: Immunity means resistance to a particular infectious agent; it can follow vaccination or recovery from an infection.

sections.heading: How immunity is acquired
paragraphs: Vaccination helps establish protection before exposure to a disease. Recovery from a prior infection may also leave resistance to that organism. Immunity is specific: protection against one germ does not mean protection against all infections. Exposure therefore does not always result in illness, but it still requires attention and appropriate reporting.

sections.heading: Course immunization list
bullets: Hepatitis B.
Influenza: yearly.
Measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR).
Varicella vaccine or a documented history of chickenpox.
Tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis (Tdap); the material lists a 10-year interval.

sections.heading: Records and screening
paragraphs: Keep a history of childhood infectious diseases and immunizations. The course also describes TB screening before hire and annually. A screening test checks for evidence of exposure/infection; it is not itself an immunization. Immunization does not eliminate the need for PPE and hand hygiene.

objectives.objective: Summarize postexposure management of exposure to patient blood or body fluids, including completing a postexposure report.
objectives.summary: Respond to exposure promptly, continue patient care through another provider, and activate the department’s exposure process.

sections.heading: Immediate steps
bullets: Transfer patient care to another EMS provider so treatment continues.
Clean exposed skin with soap and water.
If the eyes were exposed, rinse them for 20 minutes.
Activate the department’s infection control plan and notify the designated officer.
Complete an exposure report and receive screening to determine whether the exposure was significant.

sections.heading: Follow-up
paragraphs: Evaluation determines whether postexposure treatment is indicated. The course gives examples of antiviral medications for significant HIV exposure, hepatitis B antibody testing with immune globulin when appropriate, and TB testing with treatment when indicated. A significant unprotected exposure to a highly communicable airborne disease may also require a period away from work under the infection-control plan.
An exposure report is part of the response, not a substitute for cleaning and evaluation. Do not assume either that every contact caused infection or that an apparently healthy patient poses no risk.

objectives.objective: Discuss the steps necessary to determine scene safety and to prevent work-related injuries at the scene.
objectives.summary: Scene safety starts at dispatch and continues throughout the call; do not enter a hazard that requires resources beyond your training.

sections.heading: Initial and ongoing safety
bullets: Use seat belts and appropriate PPE while responding.
Assess traffic, lighting, vehicle stability, power lines, sharp objects, leaking fluids, and signs of violence before approaching.
Park safely, mark the scene, use warning devices, and wear reflective clothing when indicated.
Request needed resources rather than becoming another patient. Continue reassessing because scene conditions can change.

sections.heading: Specific hazards
paragraphs: For hazardous materials, observe labels or placards from a distance, remain uphill and upwind, and request trained HazMat personnel. Begin care after removal/decontamination or clearance of a safe area.

Do not approach a downed electrical wire or anything it contacts until qualified personnel make it safe. Fire scenes can include smoke, toxic gases, oxygen deficiency, heat, collapse, and explosions. Violent scenes require law enforcement to secure the area before approach.

sections.heading: Prevent injury
paragraphs: Inspect gear, select protective clothing for the hazard, and follow safe operating practices. EMS safety depends on both individual actions and an agency program of hazard identification, control, training, and improvement.

objectives.objective: Describe the different types of protective clothing worn to prevent injury.
objectives.summary: Protective clothing should match the actual hazard and be inspected before you need it.

sections.heading: Equipment and purpose
bullets: Cold-weather layers: moisture-wicking inner layer, insulating middle layer, and outer protection from wind and precipitation.
Turnout/bunker gear: protection against heat, fire, sparks, and flashover.
Rescue gloves: protection from cuts, heat, and cold; they may reduce dexterity. These differ from patient-care gloves.
Helmet: top and side impact protection with a secure chin strap, especially in a fall zone. Construction helmets are poorly suited to rescue.
Boots: well-fitting, flexible, water-resistant footwear with good traction; steel toes are preferred in the material.
Eye protection: side shields for routine care; goggles and face shields when tools create hazards.
Ear protection: industrial-type foam earplugs. Skin protection: sunscreen, with SPF 15 as the minimum listed.
Body armor: fitted protection for appropriate high-risk situations.

sections.heading: Other precautions
paragraphs: Keep long hair secured and limit loose jewelry or rings that can catch on equipment. No single outfit makes an otherwise unsafe scene safe to enter.

objectives.objective: Differentiate issues concerning care of the dying patient, death, and the grieving process of family members.
objectives.summary: Dying patients need honest, respectful care; families need clear information and space to grieve in their own way.

sections.heading: Care and communication
paragraphs: Introduce yourself, explain immediate care, orient the patient, and speak honestly without grim or unprofessional comments. Allow appropriate hope without making promises. Notify family members and respect the patient’s wishes and customs.

Death may be sudden or follow a long terminal illness. Acknowledge a death privately and sincerely. Ask what practical help is needed, reinforce reality gently, and avoid claiming that you know exactly how another person feels.

sections.heading: Grief
bullets: Denial: difficulty accepting that the loss is real.
Anger/hostility: distress expressed toward others or the situation.
Bargaining: attempts to change or negotiate the outcome.
Depression: sadness, guilt, or helplessness.
Acceptance: recognition of the reality of the loss.

sections.heading: After a child’s death
paragraphs: Let the family’s response guide support. When appropriate, allow parents to see or hold the child and prepare them for what they will see. Do not overwhelm grieving people with information or force a particular reaction.

objectives.objective: Recognize the physiologic, physical, and psychological responses to stress.
objectives.summary: Stress can appear as immediate body changes, physical symptoms over time, and changes in mood or behavior.

sections.heading: Physiologic response
bullets: Faster heart rate and respirations, higher blood pressure, sweating, and cool clammy skin.
Dilated pupils, tense muscles, increased blood glucose, and reduced gastrointestinal blood flow.

sections.heading: Physical and psychological signs
bullets: Physical: fatigue, appetite changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, headaches, too little or too much sleep, and changes in activity.
Psychological/behavioral: fear, withdrawal or reduced responsiveness, depression, guilt, anger, irritability, oversensitivity, and difficulty concentrating.

sections.heading: Timing matters
paragraphs: Acute reactions occur during a stressful situation. Delayed reactions appear after the event. Cumulative reactions arise from repeated or prolonged stress.

General adaptation syndrome describes an alarm response, reaction/resistance, and then recovery or exhaustion. Short-term alertness can support performance, but ongoing stress without recovery may impair health and care. Recognize changes and use support rather than waiting for exhaustion.

objectives.objective: Explain posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and steps that can be taken, including critical incident stress management, to decrease the likelihood that PTSD will develop.
objectives.summary: PTSD can follow a psychologically distressing event and includes reexperiencing the event and strong reactions to reminders.

sections.heading: Recognize and respond
paragraphs: The course describes flashbacks or nightmares and exaggerated reactions to sounds, smells, places, or other reminders of a traumatic event. A difficult call does not automatically establish PTSD, but continuing distress warrants support and professional help.

Critical incidents can include mass-casualty events, a child’s traumatic death, a serious crash involving responders, or a coworker’s death or injury. Healthy habits, recovery time, supportive relationships, and early help support coping.

sections.heading: Critical incident stress management
paragraphs: CISM is a support process facilitated by trained professionals. It can occur formally or at an ongoing scene. Defusing occurs during or immediately after the event. Debriefing is described as occurring 24–72 hours later.

These sessions support emotional recovery and should not become an operational critique or blame exercise. If CISM is unavailable, private counseling with a mental health professional is an alternative. Seeking help is part of maintaining readiness.

objectives.objective: Identify the emotional aspects of emergency care.
objectives.summary: Emergency care affects patients, families, bystanders, and providers emotionally, even when the clinical tasks are familiar.

sections.heading: During patient care
paragraphs: Critical illness, death, injury, pain, uncertainty, and frightening surroundings can intensify fear. Even experienced providers may need to overcome personal reactions before proceeding calmly. Introduce yourself, explain what you are doing, and attend to the immediate needs of the patient.

Keep words and behavior professional. Avoid remarks that increase anxiety or suggest that a patient’s situation is hopeless. Be honest about the care being provided, respect dignity, and offer appropriate reassurance.

sections.heading: Supporting others
bullets: Allow patients to express fears and concerns instead of interrupting or dismissing them.
Locate and notify family members when appropriate.
A responsible adult accompanying an injured or critically ill child can reduce anxiety and help with care.
Respect religious practices and communicate relevant wishes to the next care team.
Recognize your own emotional response and use trusted support and counseling when needed.

sources.locator: Caring for critically ill and injured patients

objectives.objective: Recognize the stress inherent in many situations, such as mass-casualty scenes.
objectives.summary: Multiple-patient scenes and other intense incidents combine clinical demands, uncertainty, danger, and emotional pressure.

sections.heading: Common stressors
bullets: Dangerous scenes and unpredictable conditions.
Physical effort, time pressure, and psychological demands.
Critically ill, injured, dead, or dying patients.
Overpowering sights, smells, and sounds.
Multiple patients with competing needs.
Angry or distressed patients, families, and bystanders.

sections.heading: Respond professionally
paragraphs: Quickly and calmly assess what patients and bystanders are doing. Use a professional tone, courteous communication, and efficient action. A person’s reaction can be influenced by age, health, past experiences, fear of medical personnel, substance use, mental illness, medications, guilt, or cultural circumstances. Do not assume everyone will respond as you would.

Mass-casualty incidents are examples of critical incident stressors. Recognize the need for recovery and support afterward, including trained CISM or counseling. Staying outwardly calm during the call does not prove that a delayed reaction will not occur.

objectives.objective: Recognize the possibility of violent situations and the steps to take to deal with them.
objectives.summary: Assess for violence before arrival and continuously on scene; patient care begins only when the approach can be made safely.

sections.heading: Avoid and manage threats
bullets: Use dispatch information and reports from other responders, then confirm conditions with your own observation.
Request law enforcement and allow officers to secure assaults, hostage incidents, riots, or other violent scenes before approach.
Know who is in command when multiple agencies are involved.
Practice recognition of warning signs, communication, deescalation, and safe escape techniques.
Use protective equipment and restraint procedures only within training and applicable protocols.

sections.heading: Cover versus concealment
paragraphs: Cover uses an impenetrable barrier for protection. Concealment hides you from view but does not necessarily stop a projectile. Do not confuse being unseen with being protected.

sections.heading: Preserve the scene
paragraphs: If a crime scene is suspected, limit disturbance and maintain evidence unless movement or alteration is required for patient care. Remain alert even after the initial scene assessment because threats can emerge during treatment.

sources.locator: Scenes of violence and responder protection

objectives.objective: Identify behavioral emergencies.
objectives.summary: Behavior that threatens the safety of the patient or others requires recognition, scene assessment, and an appropriate request for assistance.

sections.heading: What the supplied safety material emphasizes
paragraphs: Watch for escalating agitation, aggression, threatening conduct, or a person who cannot safely cooperate with care. Such behavior can make a scene unsafe and require law enforcement, additional personnel, and medical direction.

Use calm, professional communication and practiced deescalation. Continue assessing the scene rather than focusing so narrowly on the patient that you miss changes around you. Respect the person’s dignity while maintaining responder safety.

sections.heading: If restraint becomes necessary
paragraphs: Physical or chemical restraint requires training and the applicable legal and medical authorization. It is not a routine response to every difficult interaction. The workforce safety material emphasizes coordinated operations with law enforcement and proper protective equipment.

sources.locator: Violence prevention, deescalation, and restraint training

objectives.gap: The supplied Chapter 2 material gives safety and deescalation guidance but does not provide a complete definition, cause list, or assessment algorithm for behavioral emergencies.

sections.heading: Recognize and assess agitation
bullets: Mild: upset or agitated but cooperative and rational. Moderate: irrational behavior puts people at risk. Severe: physical violence creates an immediate threat.
Consider medical illness, head injury, psychiatric illness, and drugs/alcohol. Assess safety, decision-making capacity, and self-harm risk; request law enforcement early when needed.
For cooperative patients, lower stimulation, acknowledge the crisis, identify support, and encourage safe choices.

sources.title: MIEMSS: 2026 Maryland Medical Protocols for EMS (July 20 update)

outside.note: Maryland’s 2026 Agitation protocol provides this severity framework. A behavioral presentation still requires a medical assessment; this supplement does not assign a psychiatric diagnosis.

objectives.objective: Discuss workplace issues such as cultural diversity, sexual harassment, and substance abuse.
objectives.summary: A safe workplace requires respect for differences, action against harassment, and a response to substance impairment.

sections.heading: Cultural diversity
paragraphs: Culture includes nationality as well as age, disability, sex, sexual orientation, family status, work experience, and education. Communicate sensitively and accept differences. Cultural humility means remaining curious and reflecting on your own assumptions with an open mind.

sections.heading: Sexual harassment
paragraphs: Unwelcome sexual behavior may create an employment condition, affect employment decisions, or create a hostile workplace. Quid pro quo means seeking sexual favors in exchange for a benefit such as promotion. A hostile environment may involve unwanted jokes, touching, leering, or repeated requests. The effect of the conduct matters, not only the claimed intent. Report harassment promptly and keep notes.

sections.heading: Substance abuse
paragraphs: Impairment increases accidents, tension, and poor treatment decisions. EMS services may use random or for-cause drug testing. Seek help and address concerns through the workplace process rather than ignoring a coworker’s impairment. Employee assistance programs can provide support.

objectives.objective: Identify resources for positive mental health and suicide prevention.
objectives.summary: Positive mental health depends on recovery, support, and access to professional help before stress becomes unmanageable.

sections.heading: Resources identified in class
bullets: Trusted family and friends, plus supportive relationships with colleagues.
A supervisor or other workplace support when schedules, workload, or the work environment are contributing to distress.
Employee assistance programs for support with substance use and other workplace concerns.
Trained CISM professionals after critical incidents.
Private counseling or other mental health professionals, particularly when distress persists or CISM is unavailable.

sections.heading: Build support before it is needed
paragraphs: Keep interests and relationships outside emergency services. Protect sleep, nutrition, physical activity, and time away from work. Recognize withdrawal, depression, guilt, anger, worsening sleep, burnout, and loss of compassion as reasons to seek help.

The course identifies increased suicide risk among responders and emphasizes that emotional health is as important as physical health. Support should be used rather than treating distress as something that must be concealed.

objectives.gap: The supplied material does not name a suicide-prevention hotline or provide a detailed crisis-response procedure.

sections.heading: Crisis resources
bullets: Call or text 988, or use chat at 988lifeline.org, for suicide concerns, emotional distress, or a mental health/substance use crisis. Support is available around the clock; you can contact it for yourself or about someone else.
Call 911 or go to an emergency department for immediate physical danger or a medical emergency.

If concerned about someone, ask directly about suicide, listen without judgment, help them connect to professional support, and check in afterward. Do not promise secrecy about an immediate safety threat.

sources.title: Indian Health Service: How to Talk About Suicide

objectives.objective: Define consent and how it relates to decision making.
objectives.summary: Consent is permission to provide care. Valid consent depends on the patient’s ability to understand and choose.

sections.heading: Decision-making capacity
paragraphs: A patient must be able to understand the information provided and make an informed choice about medical care. Patient autonomy is the right to make decisions about one’s own health, including decisions the EMT would not choose. Consciousness alone does not establish capacity.

sections.heading: Assess understanding
bullets: Consider legal age, cognitive limitations, dementia, intoxication, serious illness or injury, pain, and distracting injuries.
Identify hearing, visual, and language barriers that may interfere with communication.
Explain the condition, recommended care, benefits, risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.
Ask questions that let the patient show understanding. Observe whether responses and behavior are rational and consistent.
The choice should be clearly communicated and made freely rather than under pressure.

sections.heading: If capacity is uncertain
paragraphs: Do not assume an informed choice has been made. Contact medical direction and follow the applicable consent process while protecting patient and responder safety.

objectives.objective: Compare expressed consent, implied consent, and involuntary consent.
objectives.summary: Expressed, implied, and involuntary consent differ in who can give permission and the circumstances that authorize care.

sections.heading: Compare the types
bullets: Expressed consent: the patient clearly accepts treatment or transport, verbally or through an unmistakable action. It must be informed: explain treatment, risks, benefits, alternatives, and consequences of refusing.

Implied consent: an unconscious or otherwise incapable patient has a serious emergency threatening life or limb. The emergency doctrine assumes the patient would accept necessary care if able. Seek family input when time allows without delaying emergency treatment.

Involuntary consent: some patients in a mental or behavioral crisis, or unable to decide under applicable law, may require a guardian’s authorization or protective-custody procedures involving law enforcement.

sections.heading: Important limit
paragraphs: A diagnosis or disagreement does not by itself authorize treatment against someone’s wishes. Assess capacity and follow local law and medical direction. Implied consent is an emergency basis for care, not a convenience when an alert patient refuses.

objectives.objective: Discuss consent by minors for treatment or transport.
objectives.summary: For a minor, consent generally comes from a parent or legal guardian, with recognized exceptions and implied consent in true emergencies.

sections.heading: Who may authorize care
bullets: Parent or legal guardian: the usual decision maker.

Emancipated minor: a minor legally treated as an adult; criteria depend on state law. The general material gives marriage, military service, parenthood, or independence from parental support as possible criteria.
School or camp official: may act in loco parentis, meaning in place of a parent, in the relevant setting.
True emergency with no available authorization: give necessary care under implied consent rather than withholding lifesaving treatment.

sections.heading: Maryland examples taught in class
paragraphs: The course slides describe minors consenting when emancipated, married, or a parent, and for treatment related to drug or alcohol abuse, sexually transmitted infection, rape, or abuse. These are course examples of specific exceptions, not a general rule that every minor can consent to every treatment. Follow the applicable consent process and seek medical direction when uncertain.

objectives.objective: Describe local EMS system protocols for using forcible restraint.
objectives.summary: Restraint requires legal authority, a safety need, medical oversight, and continuous attention to breathing and circulation.

sections.heading: When and how
paragraphs: A patient who needs treatment and transport and poses danger to self or others may require restraint. Consult medical control, use law enforcement as indicated, and follow local laws and protocols. Unauthorized restraint can create civil and criminal liability. ALS may be requested for pharmacologic restraint.
Once applied, restraints generally remain during transport unless they are creating a risk to the patient. The priority is safe care, not simply keeping the restraints in place.

sections.heading: Prevent restraint-related asphyxia
bullets: Avoid face-down positioning or pressure on the neck, chest, or back that interferes with breathing.
Do not restrain limbs in a way that compresses the chest or airway.
Monitor airway, breathing, and circulation during and after restraint. Watch for gasping, cyanosis, struggling to breathe, or decreasing responsiveness.
If compromise develops, reassess and correct the restraint-related hazard promptly while maintaining safety.

objectives.gap: The supplied material does not include the full local forcible-restraint protocol, approved devices, or an exact application procedure.

sections.heading: Maryland physical restraint essentials
bullets: For patients older than one year under implied consent, restraint is reserved for danger to the patient or others. Ensure adequate personnel; use police assistance when available.

Use minimum necessary restraint. Position face up or on the side; never prone, hobbled, or hog-tied. Adults: four-point restraint; children under 13: three-point restraint. The protocol also describes a sheet wrap with a Reeves-type stretcher.
Continuously monitor airway; check oxygenation, vital signs, and distal circulation/movement/sensation. Record findings and the reason for restraint every 15 minutes.
Keep restraints during transport unless complications occur; obtain a physician’s written restraint order for interfacility transfer.

sources.title: MIEMSS: 2026 Maryland Medical Protocols for EMS (July 20 update)

outside.note: State protocol essentials are supplied here. Your agency’s approved devices, hands-on technique, staffing, and operational policy still require agency or instructor confirmation.

objectives.objective: Discuss the EMT’s role and obligations if a patient refuses treatment or transport.
objectives.summary: A capable adult may refuse or withdraw consent, even when refusal could cause serious harm. The EMT must support an informed decision and document it.

sections.heading: Before accepting refusal
bullets: Assess and document decision-making capacity using questions, answers, and observed behavior. Confusion, delusions, or suicidality make an informed refusal uncertain.
Explain assessment concerns, recommended treatment, treatment risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusing.
Involve online medical control and record the consultation.
Do not endanger yourself when attempting care.

sections.heading: Before leaving
bullets: Encourage acceptance of treatment or transport again.
Tell the patient or responsible decision maker that they can call 9-1-1 again if they change their mind.
Recommend contacting their physician promptly.
Request a signed refusal form and a witness.
Thoroughly document findings, explanations, the patient’s responses, capacity assessment, medical-control advice, and the refusal.

sections.heading: Key distinction
paragraphs: A signature is part of documentation; it does not replace an assessment of capacity or the discussion needed for an informed refusal.

sources.locator: Refusal and leaving a refusal scene

objectives.objective: Describe the relationship between patient communications, confidentiality, and the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
objectives.summary: Patient communications and care information are confidential, and HIPAA protects both health information and identifying information.

sections.heading: Protected information
paragraphs: History, assessment findings, treatment, and other information obtained during care are protected. PHI includes medical details and information that can identify the patient. Inappropriate disclosure can breach confidentiality and expose the provider and agency to civil or criminal consequences.

sections.heading: Appropriate sharing
paragraphs: Relevant information must reach those treating the patient. The material also recognizes release with patient authorization, a legal subpoena, necessary billing functions, and disclosures required by law. These are defined purposes, not permission for unrestricted discussion.

sections.heading: Online and off duty
paragraphs: Use the same professional respect online as in person. Do not casually post patient details or images, and do not assume removing a name makes an otherwise identifiable event appropriate to share. The public’s ability to record an event does not eliminate your professional confidentiality duty.
Protect accurate records while preserving the information needed for continuing care.

objectives.objective: Discuss the importance of do not resuscitate (DNR) orders and local protocols as they relate to the EMS environment.
objectives.summary: A DNR authorizes withholding resuscitation under the applicable protocol; it does not mean withholding all treatment.

sections.heading: Understand the documents
paragraphs: Advance directives record a capable person’s treatment wishes for a time when they cannot decide. A DNR addresses resuscitation. POLST/MOLST documents are medical orders describing acceptable life-sustaining interventions and must have the appropriate authorized provider signature. A health care proxy or durable power of attorney identifies a surrogate decision maker when the patient lacks capacity.

sections.heading: EMT responsibilities
bullets: Identify the document and follow the service’s protocol for recognition and validity.
Provide appropriate supportive measures, such as oxygen, comfort, and other authorized care, when the patient is not in cardiac arrest.
Contact medical control when an order is unclear or its application is uncertain.
The Maryland MOLST teaching example emphasizes that EMS does not follow the second portion of that form.

sections.heading: Do not substitute assumptions
paragraphs: Family wishes alone are not the same as identifying and applying a valid order. A donor card also is not a DNR.

sources.locator: DNR, POLST/MOLST, and Maryland MOLST example

objectives.gap: General document principles and a Maryland form example are supplied, but the complete local DNR/MOLST recognition and resuscitation protocol is not included.

sections.heading: Maryland MOLST options
bullets: Attempt CPR: resuscitate if cardiac or respiratory arrest occurs.
No CPR A-1: provide comprehensive treatment before arrest, including intubation when indicated and within scope; do not resuscitate after arrest.
No CPR A-2: comprehensive treatment before arrest, with no intubation. CPAP/BiPAP may be included; do not resuscitate after arrest.

No CPR B: comfort and supportive treatment before arrest, including passive oxygen, bleeding control, positioning, splinting, and authorized pain relief. No intubation or CPAP/BiPAP; do not resuscitate after arrest.
EMS follows the CPR-status orders in Section 1. Sections 2–9 are directed to other care settings and do not apply to EMS.

sections.heading: Recognize a valid order
bullets: A completed MOLST needs an authorized clinician’s signature and date. Maryland recognizes copies/electronic copies, approved MOLST or EMS/DNR identifiers, older Maryland EMS/DNR forms, and reciprocal out-of-state EMS/DNR forms.
An advance directive, a generic colored bracelet, a DNR sticker, or a family member’s verbal request alone is not an EMS DNR order.

An on-scene physician, NP, or PA, or EMS medical consultation, may give an oral DNR order. Seek medical consultation when instructions are unclear; document the order and send a copy with the patient.

sources.title: Maryland MOLST: Order Form and Instructions
MIEMSS: 2026 Maryland Medical Protocols for EMS (July 20 update)

outside.note: These are Maryland-specific orders and recognition rules. Use the current protocol and medical consultation for disputed validity, revocation, or unusual circumstances; confirm agency procedures with your instructor.

objectives.objective: Describe the physical, presumptive, and definitive signs of death.
objectives.summary: Presumptive signs suggest death; definitive signs indicate irreversible death and guide action under local protocols.

sections.heading: Presumptive signs
bullets: No response to pain; no carotid pulse or heartbeat.
No chest rise/fall or measurable systolic blood pressure.
Absent deep tendon or corneal reflexes and no pupillary reaction.
Profound cyanosis and decreased body temperature.

sections.heading: Definitive signs
bullets: Obvious mortal injury, such as decapitation.
Dependent lividity: blood settles into dependent areas, producing skin discoloration.
Rigor mortis: muscle stiffening caused by chemical changes; the course gives 2–12 hours after death.
Algor mortis: the body cools toward environmental temperature.
Putrefaction: tissue decomposition; the material gives 40–96 hours, affected by environmental conditions.

sections.heading: Scene responsibilities
paragraphs: A physician determines the cause of death. Follow local death-determination and notification protocols. Medical examiner/coroner involvement may be required for unexplained, violent, accidental, poisoning-related, criminally suspicious, infant, or child deaths. Minimize disturbance and document any findings and care already performed.

sources.locator: Presumptive and definitive signs; medical examiner cases

objectives.objective: Explain how to manage patients who are identified as organ donors.
objectives.summary: Treat an identified organ donor like any other patient: saving that patient’s life remains the priority.

sections.heading: What donor status means
paragraphs: A donor card or driver’s license may record the patient’s wish to donate organs. This information can matter to the receiving team, but it does not authorize limiting emergency care or delaying treatment. The course emphasizes that organs need oxygen as well.

sections.heading: EMT approach
bullets: Assess and provide the necessary lifesaving care for the patient’s current condition.
Maintain appropriate oxygenation and circulation as part of patient care.
Communicate the donor information during the handoff without allowing it to distract from immediate needs.
Use the usual clinical and protocol-based approach to treatment and destination.

sections.heading: Distinguish donor status from treatment orders
paragraphs: The wish to donate organs is not a DNR and is not a statement that resuscitation should be withheld. Evaluate any actual resuscitation order through its separate recognition process. Do not treat the donor as a source of organs rather than as the person needing care.

objectives.objective: Recognize the importance of medical identification devices in treating the patient.
objectives.summary: Medical identification devices can provide important history or treatment information when the patient cannot explain it.

sections.heading: Look for useful information
paragraphs: A bracelet, necklace, keychain, or wallet card may identify allergies, a significant medical condition, or a possible DNR order. Some bracelets contain a USB drive with records stored as a PDF. These clues can help focus assessment and improve communication with the receiving team.

sections.heading: Use it appropriately
bullets: Include identification devices in the patient assessment rather than relying only on spoken history.
Relate the information to the patient’s current findings and share relevant details in the handoff.
Follow the department’s policy when accessing electronic information.
If a device references a DNR or other order, follow the document/protocol recognition process.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: An unresponsive or confused patient may not be able to tell you about a condition or allergy. Medical identification supplies another information source, but it does not replace examination, immediate care, or verification of treatment-limiting orders.

sources.locator: Medical identification tags and electronic records

objectives.objective: Discuss the scope of practice and standards of care.
objectives.summary: Scope of practice defines what care you may provide; standard of care describes how that authorized care should be provided.

sections.heading: Scope of practice
paragraphs: State law usually defines the EMT’s authorized range of care. The medical director further specifies it through protocols and standing orders. Authorization may be online by radio/telephone or off-line through written directions. Exceeding scope can create negligence concerns.

sections.heading: Standard of care
paragraphs: The comparison is a reasonably prudent person with similar training and experience, working under similar circumstances with similar equipment. Standards can come from law, local custom, professional recommendations, institutional policies, textbooks, and state requirements. Local protocols may differ from a general textbook description; follow the applicable local protocol.

sections.heading: Apply both
paragraphs: Being familiar with a procedure does not make it part of your authorized scope. Conversely, permission to perform a procedure does not excuse performing it carelessly. Know the limits of your role, the relevant instructions, and the expected method of providing care.

sources.locator: Scope of practice and standards of care

objectives.objective: Describe the EMT’s legal duty to act.
objectives.summary: Duty to act is the responsibility to provide patient care when the applicable legal or professional relationship requires it.

sections.heading: When the duty exists
paragraphs: The course states that once the ambulance responds to a call, or once treatment begins, a legal duty to act exists. Beginning care establishes responsibility that cannot simply be ended without an appropriate plan for continuing care. Paid and volunteer status do not remove the obligation once it exists.

sections.heading: Off-duty situations
paragraphs: In most cases, an off-duty EMT who happens upon a crash is not legally required to stop, but local law and service policy determine the actual rule. Do not assume a universal off-duty exemption or obligation.

sections.heading: Connect it to care
paragraphs: Duty is one of the four elements needed for negligence. After care starts, maintain it until appropriate transfer or another lawful conclusion. Ensure a qualified provider actually accepts responsibility rather than assuming arrival at a hospital or another responder’s presence ends your duty. Protect personal safety and operate within training and protocols.

objectives.objective: Discuss the issues of negligence, abandonment, assault and battery, and kidnapping and their implications for the EMT.
objectives.summary: These legal concepts describe different failures: unreasonable care, ending care improperly, threatening or touching without authority, and confinement or transport without authority.

sections.heading: Negligence
paragraphs: Negligence is failure to provide the care a similarly trained person would provide in similar circumstances. All four elements are required: duty, breach of duty, damages, and causation. A poor outcome alone does not establish all four.

sections.heading: Abandonment
paragraphs: Abandonment is unilateral termination of care without patient consent and without arranging competent continuing care. Once care begins, it continues until an equally competent provider accepts responsibility. Obtain the receiving person’s signature on the care record. Physical arrival at the ED does not complete a handoff by itself.

sections.heading: Assault, battery, and kidnapping
bullets: Assault: unlawfully causing fear of immediate bodily harm, including a threat to force transport without authority.
Battery: unlawful touching, including treatment without valid consent or another lawful basis.
Kidnapping: seizing, confining, or carrying someone away by force. False imprisonment is unauthorized confinement.

sections.heading: Prevent problems
paragraphs: Assess capacity, obtain the appropriate consent or authorization, respect valid withdrawal, follow protocols, and document decisions and transfers.

sources.locator: Negligence; abandonment; assault, battery, and kidnapping

objectives.objective: Explain the reporting requirements for special situations, including abuse, drug- or felony-related injuries, childbirth, and crime scenes.
objectives.summary: Special reporting duties vary by jurisdiction; the EMT must recognize the situation, provide care, document facts, and use the required reporting process.

sections.heading: Situations identified in class
bullets: Suspected child abuse, elder abuse, or abuse of another at-risk adult.
Felony-related and drug-related injuries, assaults, domestic violence, and sexual assault/rape.
Childbirth, attempted suicide, and dog bites.
Certain communicable diseases and infectious exposures.
Transport in restraints, crime scenes, and deceased patients.

sections.heading: What the EMT does
paragraphs: Treat immediate needs without attempting to prove who caused an injury. Record objective observations, relevant statements, findings, and actions accurately. Report through the local process, which may involve receiving hospital staff, law enforcement, the supervisor, or another designated authority. Documentation does not substitute for a required notification.

At a possible crime scene, preserve evidence and minimize unnecessary disturbance, while making changes necessary for patient treatment. Document those changes. Do not promise secrecy when mandatory reporting applies.

sources.locator: Special Mandatory Reporting Requirements: scene of a crime

objectives.gap: The material lists reportable categories but does not supply the complete local reporting statutes, contacts, deadlines, or forms.

sections.heading: Maryland reporting rules
bullets: Suspected child abuse/neglect: notify the local department of social services or appropriate law enforcement as soon as possible orally. Submit a written report to the local department within 48 hours of the encounter that raised suspicion, with a copy to the local State’s Attorney. Include the child’s identity/location, caregiver information, observations, and relevant statements when known.

Suspected abuse, neglect, self-neglect, or exploitation of a vulnerable adult: notify the local department as soon as possible by telephone, direct communication, writing, or the statewide reporting hotline. Report the person’s location, incapacity, suspected harm, and relevant facts. Do not assume the child-reporting 48-hour rule applies to adults.

Gunshot injuries: Maryland Health–General §20-703 requires prompt reporting by the named treating professionals or hospital head to the county sheriff, county police, or State Police. The statute names physicians, pharmacists, dentists, nurses, and hospital heads; this provision does not name EMTs, so confirm the agency’s designated notification process.

Childbirth: Health–General §4-208 generally requires birth registration within five calendar days and assigns responsibility by birth location and attending clinician/individual. For an EMS delivery, document the birth and hand off information; confirm who completes registration under the agency and receiving facility process.

sections.heading: What still depends on the jurisdiction
paragraphs: The class’s broad list is a set of situations needing attention, not proof that every category has one statewide EMT reporting deadline. Agency instructions and applicable law determine notification for drug-related or other felony injuries, sexual assault, bites, communicable diseases, and crime scenes. Preserve observations and necessary treatment changes in the patient report; confirm the designated contacts, forms, and notification route.

sources.title: Maryland Family Law §5-704: Child Abuse/Neglect Reports
Maryland Family Law §14-302: Vulnerable Adult Reports

outside.note: Maryland statutory examples are supplied. Agency contacts, forms, and rules for categories not resolved here remain matters for the agency/instructor; do not infer a universal duty from the class list.

objectives.objective: Define ethics and morality, and discuss their implications for the EMT.
objectives.summary: Ethics concerns right and wrong, moral duties, and professional behavior; morality concerns the code of conduct that shapes conscience and conduct.

sections.heading: Related terms
bullets: Ethics: the principles used to evaluate right and wrong and ideal professional behavior.
Morality: the code influencing character, conduct, and conscience.
Bioethics: ethical questions that arise specifically in health care.
Applied ethics: putting ethical principles into professional conduct.

sections.heading: EMT implications
paragraphs: The EMT has responsibilities to the patient, public, coworkers, and self in addition to legal duties. Respect, honesty, compassion, confidentiality, and appropriate care are practical expressions of those responsibilities.

Ethical dilemmas can involve refusal, end-of-life decisions, or conflicts between personal beliefs and professional obligations. Evaluate both your own values and the profession’s standards. Use rules, laws, policies, and medical direction to guide decisions rather than allowing personal preference alone to determine care.
A legal rule tells you an obligation or limit; ethical reasoning also asks whether your behavior serves the patient and respects the people involved.

objectives.objective: Describe the roles and responsibilities of the EMT in court.
objectives.summary: An EMT may appear in court as a witness or defendant in a civil or criminal case; preparation starts with accurate records and the service’s legal process.

sections.heading: When contacted
bullets: If subpoenaed, notify the service director and legal counsel immediately.
As a witness, remain neutral and review the patient care report before appearing. Describe facts you know rather than guessing or taking sides.
As a defendant, obtain an attorney; a civil-case attorney is generally provided through the service. A criminal charge requires experienced criminal representation.

sections.heading: Process and terminology
paragraphs: Discovery allows both sides to obtain information. Interrogatories are written questions; depositions involve oral questioning. Many cases settle after discovery rather than going to trial.
Possible defenses discussed include statute of limitations, governmental immunity, and contributory negligence. These are legal issues for counsel, not automatic guarantees of protection.

Compensatory damages reimburse injury-related losses. Punitive damages aim to deter intentional or recklessly unsafe conduct and are not commonly awarded for ordinary negligence. Complete, factual documentation supports truthful testimony and evaluation of the care provided.

sources.locator: The EMT in court; discovery; trial

objectives.objective: Explain the purpose of medical terminology.
objectives.summary: Medical terminology gives health care teams a shared, precise language for describing the body, patient findings, conditions, and care.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: EMTs use this language in verbal handoffs, communication with medical control and other responders, and written patient care reports. A shared meaning helps the next clinician understand exactly what was found and what was done.
bullets: Understand key terms, abbreviations, and symbols before using them.
Anatomic terms identify locations consistently, regardless of who is viewing the patient.
Learning word parts helps you interpret unfamiliar terms instead of memorizing every complete word.
Accurate spelling matters: a small change can describe an entirely different problem.
Use terminology that other members of the care team understand; unfamiliar shorthand can create errors.

objectives.objective: Identify the four components that comprise a medical term.
objectives.summary: The four components are the word root, prefix, suffix, and combining vowel.

sections.heading: Building blocks
bullets: Word root: the foundation and essential meaning, often a body part, organ, or system. A term may have more than one root.
Prefix: appears before the root and modifies it, often describing location or intensity. Not every term has a prefix.
Suffix: appears after the root and commonly describes a condition, disease, procedure, or part of speech.
Combining vowel: joins a root to another root or a suffix and makes pronunciation easier. The usual vowel is o; i and e also occur. A root written with its combining vowel is a combining form.

sections.heading: Rules
