paragraphs: The prefix, when present, is at the beginning and the suffix is at the end. Use a combining vowel before a suffix beginning with a consonant, and between two roots even when the second root begins with a vowel.
bullets: Changing or deleting a component can change the meaning; recognize the actual parts rather than guessing from how a word sounds.

sources.locator: II. Anatomy of a Medical Term; III. Word Building Rules

objectives.objective: Describe the following directional terms: anterior (ventral), posterior (dorsal), right, left, superior, inferior, proximal, distal, medial, lateral, superficial, and deep.
objectives.summary: Directional terms describe one structure relative to another using the patient’s anatomy, not the observer’s viewpoint.

sections.heading: Required terms
bullets: Anterior (ventral): the front or belly side. Posterior (dorsal): the back or spinal side.
Right and left: always the patient’s right and left. Facing a patient does not reverse the side you document.
Superior: nearer the head. Inferior: nearer the feet.
Proximal: closer to the trunk or attachment of an extremity. Distal: farther from the trunk or toward the free end.
Medial: closer to the midline. Lateral: farther from the midline.
Superficial: on or nearer the skin. Deep: farther inside the body or away from the skin.

sections.heading: Related vocabulary
bullets: Palmar: palm surface of the hand. Plantar: bottom of the foot. Apex: tip of a structure; plural apices.
Bilateral: on both sides. Unilateral: on one side.
Flexion bends a joint; extension straightens it. Adduction moves toward the midline; abduction moves away.

sections.heading: Apply the reference point
paragraphs: An elbow is proximal to the wrist, while the fingers are distal to the elbow. The nose is medial to the eyes, while the ears are lateral to the nose. Directional words state a relationship; they do not describe the patient’s current position in the room.

sources.locator: VI. Common Direction, Movement, and Position Terms

objectives.objective: Describe the prone, supine, Fowler, and semi-Fowler positions of the body.
objectives.summary: Prone and supine describe lying positions; Fowler and semi-Fowler describe upright or partly upright positions.

sections.heading: Positions
bullets: Prone: lying face down.
Supine: lying face up on the back.
Fowler: upright or semi-reclining with the head elevated; used to help breathing and airway control. High-Fowler is about 90 degrees.
Semi-Fowler: a partly sitting position with the stretcher back elevated about 45 degrees. The lecture also describes a 30–45 degree range.

sections.heading: Keep position and direction separate
paragraphs: Supine tells you how the whole patient is lying. Anterior and posterior tell you which body surface is being described. A patient’s right arm remains the right arm in any position.
bullets: The recovery position places the patient on the side. Its use depends on patient condition and suspected injuries.
Identify the actual position rather than using Fowler and semi-Fowler interchangeably; the amount of elevation differs.

objectives.objective: Break down the meaning of a medical term based on the components of the term.
objectives.summary: Define the suffix first, then the prefix if present, then the root. Combine the meanings into a clear description.

sections.heading: Worked examples
bullets: Nephr/o/pathy: -pathy = disease; nephr = kidney; o joins the parts. Nephropathy means kidney disease.
Dys/ur/ia: -ia = condition; dys- = difficult, painful, or abnormal; ur = urine. Dysuria means difficult or painful urination.
Hyper/emesis: hyper- = excessive; emesis = vomiting. Hyperemesis means excessive vomiting.
An/alges/ic: -ic = pertaining to; an- = without; alges = pain. Analgesic means pertaining to absence of pain.
Tachy/card/ia: tachy- = fast; card = heart; -ia = condition. Tachycardia means an abnormally fast heart rate.

sections.heading: Avoid look-alike errors
paragraphs: Dysphasia concerns difficulty speaking; dysphagia concerns difficulty swallowing. The spelling of the ending changes the finding. Use anatomy and context to check that the interpretation fits.
bullets: A combining vowel eases pronunciation; it does not supply a separate disease or location meaning.
Keep the order of the complete term in mind, but work backward from the ending when decoding it.

objectives.objective: Identify error-prone medical abbreviations and symbols.
objectives.summary: Error-prone shorthand is shorthand whose meaning may be misread or misunderstood by other clinicians.

sections.heading: Safe use
paragraphs: Use only standard, commonly understood abbreviations and symbols accepted in the service area. A shortcut understood by one crew may not be understood by another agency, a receiving clinician, or someone reading the report later. Written shorthand needs the same clarity as a verbal handoff.
bullets: If a shortcut is unfamiliar or ambiguous, use the full wording.
Know your agency’s accepted usage before documenting it.
Abbreviations shorten words; acronyms shorten groups of words, commonly using initial letters.
The class identifies the Joint Commission and Institute for Safe Medication Practices as organizations that maintain do-not-use lists.

objectives.gap: The supplied class materials explain the risk and refer to do-not-use lists, but do not supply a named list of individual error-prone abbreviations or symbols.

sections.heading: Common error-prone shorthand
bullets: U/u or IU: write “units”; the shorthand can resemble numbers or IV.
QD/q.d. and QOD/q.o.d.: write “daily” or “every other day”; similar letters and punctuation invite mix-ups.
D/C: spell out “discharge” or “discontinue” so the intended action is unmistakable.
IN, SC, or SQ: prefer “intranasal” and “subcutaneous” in medication communication to avoid route confusion.
cc and µg: use mL and mcg for clearer units.
For a dose below one, include the leading zero: 0.5 mg. For a whole-number dose, omit a trailing decimal zero: 1 mg. A missed decimal can create a tenfold error.
In medication instructions, spell out comparison signs and arrows—“more than,” “less than,” “increase,” or “decrease”—when misreading could change treatment.
Write complete drug names and leave space between the drug, dose, and units.

objectives.objective: Interpret selected medical abbreviations and symbols.
objectives.summary: Interpret shorthand using its accepted meaning and the context in which it is used.

sections.heading: Examples available in the material
bullets: CPR: cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
RUQ: right upper quadrant of the abdomen.
LUQ: left upper quadrant.
RLQ: right lower quadrant.
LLQ: left lower quadrant.

sections.heading: Abdominal quadrants
paragraphs: An imaginary vertical and horizontal line through the navel divides the abdomen into four quadrants. Right and left remain the patient’s sides. RUQ includes the liver and gallbladder; LUQ includes the stomach and spleen; RLQ includes the appendix and intestinal structures; LLQ includes intestinal structures.
bullets: Use only shorthand whose meaning is accepted and widely understood.
If a symbol or abbreviation has an unclear meaning, write the full term rather than guessing.

objectives.gap: The supplied files do not include the referenced master tables or a comprehensive set of abbreviation and symbol interpretations. Only explicit class examples are included.

sections.heading: Selected abbreviations to recognize
bullets: Assessment: BP means blood pressure; HR means heart rate; RR means respiratory rate; VS means vital signs.
Clinical notes: Hx means history; Dx means diagnosis; Sx means symptom; Pt means patient.
Tests: ECG or EKG means electrocardiogram; CBC means complete blood count; CXR means chest x-ray.
Routes: PO means by mouth; IV means intravenous; IM means intramuscular.
Medication frequency: BID means twice daily; TID means three times daily; QID means four times daily; PRN means as needed.
Common conditions: MI means myocardial infarction; CHF means congestive heart failure; HTN means hypertension; NKDA means no known drug allergies.
Units: mg means milligram; mL means milliliter; mcg means microgram. Distinguish mass units from volume units when reading a dose.

sections.heading: Context matters
paragraphs: This is a selected reference, not a replacement for the missing textbook master table. An abbreviation can have multiple meanings. Interpret it in context and clarify uncertainty before acting. Some older lists include QD/QOD; understand what they mean, but write out daily/every other day because of their medication-error risk.

objectives.objective: Identify the body’s topographic anatomy, including the anatomic position and the planes of the body.
objectives.summary: Topographic anatomy uses a standard anatomic position and imaginary body planes to describe locations consistently.

sections.heading: Position and planes
bullets: Anatomic position: standing facing forward, arms at the sides, palms facing forward.
Coronal or frontal plane: separates front from back.
Sagittal plane: separates left from right; a midsagittal plane divides equal left and right halves.
Transverse or axial plane: separates upper from lower sections.

sections.heading: From small structures to whole systems
paragraphs: Cells are the foundation of the body. Cells with common functions form tissues; groups of tissues form organs; related organs work together as body systems. Anatomy studies structure, while physiology studies normal function.
bullets: Topographic descriptions refer to the patient’s anatomy rather than where the observer stands.
Use body planes along with terms such as medial/lateral and proximal/distal to identify the specific region.

sources.locator: I. Introduction; II. Topographic Anatomy; III. From Cells to Systems

objectives.objective: Identify the anatomy and physiology of the skeletal system.
objectives.summary: The skeleton supports the body, protects organs, permits movement, stores calcium, and helps produce blood cells.

sections.heading: Organization and axial skeleton
bullets: The skeleton has 206 bones. The axial skeleton includes the skull, facial bones, thoracic cage, and vertebral column. The appendicular skeleton includes limbs and their attachments; the pelvis includes contributions from both.
Skull landmarks include frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital regions; maxillae form the fixed upper jaw, the mandible the movable lower jaw, and zygomas the cheekbones. Orbits protect the eyes.
Spine: 33 vertebrae in five regions—7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, and 4 fused coccygeal. Ligaments connect vertebrae and disks separate and protect them.
Thorax: 12 thoracic vertebrae and 12 pairs of ribs. Sternum parts are manubrium, body, and xiphoid process. The cage protects the heart, lungs, and great vessels.

sections.heading: Appendicular skeleton
bullets: Shoulder girdle: clavicle and scapula connect with the humerus. The humerus supports the arm.
Forearm: radius on the lateral/thumb side; ulna on the medial/little-finger side. Wrist bones are carpals; hand bones metacarpals; fingers phalanges.
Each hip bone comprises ilium, ischium, and pubis. The pubic symphysis joins the pubic bones. The femoral head meets the acetabulum.

Femur supports the thigh; its trochanters anchor muscles. The knee is a hinge joint. Tibia and fibula form the lower leg. Their distal ends meet the talus at the ankle; the foot has tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges.

sections.heading: Joints
bullets: A joint is where bones meet. Ligaments connect bone to bone; tendons connect muscle to bone.
Cartilage cushions articulating ends. A joint capsule encloses the joint; its synovial lining produces lubricating fluid.
Ball-and-socket joints permit rotation and bending; hinge joints permit flexion and extension. Symphyses permit only slight movement.

sources.locator: IV. The Skeletal System: Anatomy; The Skeletal System: Physiology

objectives.objective: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the musculoskeletal system.
objectives.summary: Muscles and the skeleton work together to provide form, upright posture, movement, and protection.

sections.heading: Three types of muscle
bullets: Skeletal muscle attaches to bones, makes up most muscle mass, and is under voluntary control. It often works in antagonistic pairs, such as biceps and triceps.
Smooth muscle is involuntary and is found in structures such as blood vessels and intestines.
Cardiac muscle is specialized involuntary muscle found only in the heart.

sections.heading: How the system functions
paragraphs: Muscle contraction and relaxation move the body and allow interaction with the environment. Tendons attach muscle to bone, transmitting the pull that produces movement at joints. Ligaments stabilize joints by connecting bones to other bones.
bullets: Movement produces heat as a by-product. Shivering uses muscle activity to generate heat when cold.
Muscle also protects structures beneath it and helps maintain posture.
Voluntary means consciously controlled; it does not mean that every muscle action needs deliberate attention. Smooth and cardiac activity do not require conscious commands.

sources.locator: Joints; V–VI. Musculoskeletal System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Discuss the anatomy and physiology of the respiratory system.
objectives.summary: Ventilation moves air; respiration exchanges gases. Both are necessary to supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: Airway and lungs
bullets: Air enters through the nose or mouth and passes through the pharynx. The larynx is the dividing landmark between upper and lower airways. The epiglottis helps prevent food and liquid from entering the trachea.
The thyroid cartilage is anterior on the larynx; cricoid cartilage lies below it; the cricothyroid membrane lies between them.
The trachea divides at the carina into right and left main bronchi, then smaller bronchi and bronchioles ending in alveoli. Alveoli are gas-exchange surfaces.
Visceral pleura covers lungs; parietal pleura lines the chest wall. Fluid in the potential space between them eases movement.

sections.heading: Breathing mechanics
paragraphs: During inhalation, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles contract, thoracic volume increases, and pressure falls so air enters. Inhalation is active. During normal quiet exhalation, these muscles relax, volume returns toward resting size, and air exits; this is passive.
bullets: The diaphragm is the primary breathing muscle. Accessory muscles include cervical, pectoral, abdominal, and intercostal muscles.
Diffusion moves oxygen and carbon dioxide from higher to lower concentration across alveolar-capillary and tissue surfaces.

sections.heading: Control and volumes
bullets: The medulla initiates breathing and signals the diaphragm through the phrenic nerve. Rising carbon dioxide and decreasing pH are primary stimuli; the pons modifies depth and pattern during stress.
Tidal volume is air per breath, generally about 500 mL in an adult. Minute ventilation = respiratory rate × tidal volume.

Inspiratory reserve is additional inspired air after a normal breath; expiratory reserve is additional forced exhaled air. Residual volume remains after exhalation. Dead space contributes little or no gas exchange.

sections.heading: Assess adequacy
bullets: Normal breathing has appropriate rate and depth, regular rhythm, equal chest rise, and clear bilateral sounds.

Labored effort, retractions, accessory muscle use, pale or cyanotic skin, cool damp skin, or tripod positioning raise concern. Adult rates below 12 or above 20/min require assessment in context. Rate alone does not establish adequate ventilation.

sources.locator: VII–VIII. Respiratory System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Discuss the anatomy and physiology of the circulatory system.
objectives.summary: Circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients, removes wastes, and maintains tissue perfusion through coordinated heart, vessel, and blood functions.

sections.heading: Flow through the circuits
paragraphs: Body → venae cavae → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body. Valves guide one-way flow. Coronary arteries supply the myocardium.
bullets: Pulmonary circulation connects the right heart, lungs, and left heart. Systemic circulation connects the left heart, body tissues, and right heart.
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it. Direction, rather than oxygen content, defines them. Pulmonary arteries carry oxygen-poor blood and pulmonary veins oxygen-rich blood.

Arteries narrow into arterioles, then capillaries; venules and veins collect returning blood. Thin capillary walls permit tissue exchange. The superior vena cava returns upper-body blood; the inferior vena cava returns lower-body blood.

sections.heading: Pump and pressure
bullets: The left ventricle is a thicker high-pressure pump for the body; the right ventricle pumps at lower pressure to the lungs.
Electrical sequence: SA node → AV node → bundle of His → Purkinje fibers → coordinated ventricular contraction.
Stroke volume is blood per beat. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Typical adult pulse is 60–100/min.
Systole is contraction and ejection; diastole is relaxation and filling. Systolic pressure is the high point, diastolic pressure the low point of the pressure wave.
Perfusion is enough blood flow to meet cell needs; hypoperfusion or shock is inadequate flow. Mean arterial pressure relates to cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance: MAP = CO × SVR.

sections.heading: Blood and control
bullets: Plasma carries water, proteins, nutrients, gases, and wastes. Red cells contain oxygen-carrying hemoglobin; white cells fight infection; platelets begin clot formation. Blood also contributes to pH control.
The highly vascular spleen filters old blood cells, bacteria, and foreign material; blunt injury can cause significant bleeding.

Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate/force through beta-1 effects, constricts vessels through alpha effects, and dilates bronchi through beta-2 effects. Parasympathetic stimulation slows and weakens the heartbeat.
Baroreceptors sense pressure changes. With blood loss, faster pumping and vasoconstriction compensate until the loss exceeds the system’s ability to maintain perfusion.

sources.locator: IX–X. Circulatory System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Discuss the anatomy and physiology of the nervous system.
objectives.summary: The central nervous system processes and coordinates information; peripheral nerves carry signals to and from the body.

sections.heading: Central nervous system
bullets: CNS: brain and spinal cord. The cerebrum is the largest brain region and supports higher functions.
Frontal lobe: personality, judgment, planning, concentration, and problem solving. Parietal: spatial recognition. Occipital: vision. Temporal: hearing, taste, and understanding words.
Cerebellum: balance, coordination, and posture.
Brainstem: midbrain, pons, and medulla; regulates essential cardiac/respiratory functions and consciousness. The reticular activating system helps regulate consciousness.
Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord and helps clear impurities. Carotid arteries supply the head; jugular veins drain it.

The spinal cord extends from the brainstem through the foramen magnum, is protected by the vertebral column, and ends around the second lumbar vertebra. It carries messages between the brain and body.

sections.heading: Peripheral nervous system
bullets: Sensory nerves carry information from the body toward the CNS. Motor nerves carry commands from the CNS to muscles.
The somatic system governs voluntary activities such as walking, talking, and writing.
The autonomic system governs automatic functions. Its sympathetic division supports stress responses; its parasympathetic division counters these effects.
Damage at different levels can alter movement, sensation, consciousness, or essential automatic functions because different structures have different jobs.

sources.locator: XI. Nervous System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the integumentary system.
objectives.summary: Skin protects against the environment, regulates temperature, and carries sensory information to the brain.

sections.heading: Layers and structures
bullets: Epidermis: the superficial, watertight protective layer. Its germinal layer produces new cells; the outer stratum corneum consists of dead cells that are shed and replaced.
Dermis: the deeper skin layer containing vessels, sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles.
Subcutaneous tissue: fat beneath the skin; provides insulation and an energy reserve.

sections.heading: Functions
paragraphs: The skin is the body’s largest single organ. The barrier helps keep harmful material out and moisture in. Sweat glands contribute to cooling, and sebaceous glands produce protective oils. Sensory structures transmit environmental information so the body can respond to its surroundings.
bullets: Keep the two skin layers distinct from the subcutaneous tissue below them.
Damage to the skin can compromise barrier function and temperature control, rather than being only a surface problem.

sources.locator: XII–XIII. Integumentary System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Explain the anatomy and physiology of the digestive system.
objectives.summary: Digestion breaks food into usable nutrients, absorbs them into circulation, and eliminates remaining waste.

sections.heading: Food pathway
paragraphs: Mouth → oropharynx → esophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine → rectum → anus. Muscular action propels food, while secretions support chemical breakdown.
bullets: Mouth: lips, cheeks, gums, teeth, tongue, and palate; saliva moistens food and begins digestion.
Esophagus: collapsible muscular tube carrying food to the stomach. Stomach: stores food and passes it into the bowel.
Small intestine: duodenum, jejunum, ileum; digestive secretions and absorption make nutrients available.

Large intestine: cecum, colon, rectum; final absorption of water and remaining material forms stool. The rectum stores feces and anal sphincters control release. Appendix opens into the cecum and can become inflamed or obstructed.

sections.heading: Accessory organs
bullets: Liver: filters harmful substances; makes clotting factors and plasma components; stores sugar/starch for energy; produces bile for fat digestion.
Gallbladder stores bile; bile ducts carry it into the duodenum.
Pancreas: exocrine tissue makes enzymes for fat, starch, and protein digestion; endocrine islets make insulin and glucagon.

sections.heading: Locations and nutrient use
bullets: RUQ: liver, gallbladder, part of colon. LUQ: stomach, spleen, part of colon. RLQ: cecum and ascending colon. LLQ: descending and sigmoid colon. Some organs span several quadrants.
Kidneys and pancreas are retroperitoneal—behind the abdominal cavity. The spleen is a blood-filtering organ in the LUQ rather than part of the food pathway.
Chemical digestion yields sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids. Absorbed products travel to the liver for processing/storage and into the circulation for distribution.

sources.locator: XIV–XV. Digestive System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Describe the anatomy and the physiology of the lymphatic system.
objectives.summary: The lymphatic system supports immune defense and circulation, including tissue fluid balance and removal of harmful material.

sections.heading: Parts and functions
bullets: Lymph is thin, straw-colored fluid moving through a network of lymph vessels.
Lymph vessels provide an auxiliary pathway alongside blood circulation and help remove excess tissue fluid and waste.
Lymph nodes are small oval structures along vessels that filter lymph and trap harmful substances, including bacteria.
The spleen filters blood and contributes to defense against infection.
The thymus helps develop immune cells called T cells.

sections.heading: How the functions connect
paragraphs: This system links fluid transport with immune surveillance. Lymph flowing through vessels passes through filtering nodes. Filtering and immune-cell activity help the body recognize and remove harmful material, while fluid movement supports the balance between tissues and circulation.
bullets: Distinguish lymph-node filtering of lymph from spleen filtering of blood.
The system is supportive of both circulation and immunity; it is not an isolated transport route with no defense function.

sources.locator: XVI. Lymphatic System: Anatomy and Physiology
Lymphatic components and tissue fluid balance

objectives.objective: Discuss the anatomy and physiology of the endocrine system.
objectives.summary: Endocrine glands release hormones directly into blood to communicate with target organs and regulate body functions.

sections.heading: Hormone control
paragraphs: Each gland produces one or more hormones, and each hormone has specific effects on organs, tissues, or processes. The brain helps control release. Primary and secondary feedback loops adjust secretion to maintain balance when hormone levels change.
bullets: Hormones help regulate growth, energy use, balance, and responses to stress.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine support sympathetic stress responses, including faster, stronger heart activity and vascular constriction.
The pancreas has both digestive and hormonal functions. Its endocrine islets produce insulin and glucagon for blood-glucose regulation.
The exocrine pancreas releases digestive enzymes; endocrine products enter the bloodstream. These are different destinations and functions.

sections.heading: Disease connection
paragraphs: Too much or too little hormone can disturb normal function. Diabetes is the class example of disease associated with problems in insulin-related glucose control.

objectives.gap: The supplied lecture explains hormone signaling and gives examples, but does not provide detailed functions for every endocrine gland shown in the diagram.

sections.heading: Major glands and what they do
bullets: Hypothalamus and pituitary: the hypothalamus controls pituitary output. The anterior pituitary releases growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, gonadotropins, and prolactin. These regulate growth, other glands, reproduction, and milk production.
Posterior pituitary: releases ADH, which reduces water loss through the kidneys, and oxytocin, which promotes uterine contraction and milk ejection.
Pineal gland: lies in the brain and releases melatonin, which helps regulate daily physiologic rhythms.

Thyroid: lies below the larynx on either side of the trachea. Its T3 and T4 hormones regulate how the body uses energy (metabolism), affecting nearly every organ, including the heart. Calcitonin helps lower blood calcium.
Parathyroids: small glands on the posterior thyroid. Their hormone, PTH, raises blood calcium when it is low.
Thymus: lies behind the sternum and supports T-cell maturation for immune defense. Its hormone thymosin contributes to lymphocyte maturation.

Adrenals: sit above the kidneys. The outer cortex produces cortisol, aldosterone, and small amounts of sex hormones. Cortisol supports increased blood glucose; aldosterone conserves sodium and water. The inner medulla releases epinephrine and norepinephrine during sympathetic stress responses.
Pancreatic islets: endocrine cell groups in the pancreas. Alpha cells release glucagon when glucose is low; beta cells release insulin when glucose is high.

Testes and ovaries: produce reproductive cells and hormones. Testosterone supports male reproductive development; estrogen and progesterone support female reproductive development and changes in the uterine lining.

NIH/NCI SEER — Thyroid and parathyroid glands

objectives.objective: Describe the anatomy and physiology of the urinary system.
objectives.summary: The urinary system filters wastes from blood and helps regulate water, salt, and pH balance.

sections.heading: Urine pathway
paragraphs: Kidneys → ureters → urinary bladder → urethra → outside the body. The paired kidneys form urine; the two ureters carry it to the bladder; the bladder stores it until it leaves through the urethra.
bullets: Kidneys are solid organs in the retroperitoneal space. They remove toxic waste and regulate the balance of water and salts.
A ureter runs from each kidney into the bladder. Ureters transport urine; they do not store it.
The bladder lies in the pelvic cavity immediately behind the pubic symphysis.
The urethra is the outlet from the bladder to the exterior. Do not confuse urethra with ureter.

sections.heading: System functions
paragraphs: Waste elimination is only one role. Fluid and pH regulation connect kidney function with circulation and cellular stability. The blood must reach the kidneys for filtering, and the resulting urine must have a route out of the body.

sources.locator: XVIII. Urinary System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.objective: Discuss the anatomy and physiology of the genital system.
objectives.summary: The genital system supports reproduction. The class identifies male and female structures and their general pelvic relationships.

sections.heading: Male anatomy
bullets: Structures: testicles, epididymis, vasa deferentia, prostate gland, seminal vesicles, and penis.
The prostate gland and seminal vesicles are within the pelvic cavity. The class contrasts them with the external male genital structures.
The pictured structures include the scrotum and glans, as well as nearby urinary structures; the ureter and bladder belong to the urinary pathway.

sections.heading: Female anatomy
bullets: Structures: ovaries, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix, and vagina.
These reproductive organs are within the pelvic cavity; external structures include the clitoris and labia.
Front and side views describe the same system from different perspectives. The cervix is shown between the uterus and vagina.

sections.heading: Scope
paragraphs: The reproductive system creates the conditions for new life. Distinguish genital structures from urinary structures even when they appear together in a diagram.

sources.locator: XIX. Genital System: Anatomy and Physiology

objectives.gap: The supplied class text identifies organs and the system’s reproductive role but does not explain each reproductive organ’s individual physiology.

sections.heading: Male organ functions
bullets: Testes: produce sperm and testosterone. The scrotum keeps the testes cooler than the body core, supporting viable sperm production.
Epididymis: coiled duct where sperm mature and are stored. The vas deferens transports sperm toward the ejaculatory ducts and urethra.

Seminal vesicles: add fluid containing nutrients for sperm. The prostate adds fluid supporting sperm movement; bulbourethral glands add lubricating fluid and help neutralize residual urethral acidity.
Penis: contains erectile tissue and delivers semen through the urethra.

sections.heading: Female organ functions
bullets: Ovaries: develop egg cells and produce estrogen and progesterone.
Fallopian tubes: receive the ovulated egg and move it toward the uterus through ciliary motion and smooth-muscle activity. Fertilization usually occurs here.

Uterus: muscular organ supporting fetal development. Its inner lining, the endometrium, changes during the menstrual cycle and partially sheds during menstruation. The cervix is its lower portion opening into the vagina.
Vagina: passage for menstrual flow, intercourse, and childbirth.
Vulva: external genital structures, including the labia and clitoris. The clitoris contains erectile tissue and responds to sexual stimulation.

objectives.objective: Describe the life support chain, aerobic metabolism, and anaerobic metabolism.
objectives.summary: The life support chain brings oxygen and nutrients to cells and removes their waste so metabolism can continue.

sections.heading: Linked steps
paragraphs: Respiration supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide. Circulation carries oxygen and nutrients to tissue and carries wastes away. Diffusion moves these substances across the relevant membranes. Cells use available nutrients to make chemical energy stored and used as ATP.
bullets: Aerobic metabolism uses oxygen.
When oxygen is limited, cells switch to anaerobic metabolism. Lactic acid and other wastes can accumulate.
Accumulation makes the environment acidic and toxic, impairing cells and eventually causing cell death.
A problem in either breathing or perfusion can interrupt cellular oxygen delivery, even if the other part of the chain works.

sections.heading: Why the chain matters
paragraphs: Shock reduces blood and oxygen delivery. Respiratory compromise reduces effective gas movement or exchange. Both can force anaerobic metabolism and organ dysfunction. Some cellular injury may be reversible if normal perfusion returns in time. Brain cells are especially vulnerable when glucose supply falls markedly.

sources.locator: XX. Life Support Chain; XXI. Shock and Alteration of cellular metabolism

objectives.objective: Define pathophysiology.
objectives.summary: Pathophysiology is the study of the functional changes that occur with disease or a syndrome.

sections.heading: Structure, normal function, altered function
bullets: Anatomy asks what the structure is. Physiology asks how it normally works. Pathophysiology asks how illness changes that function.
Respiratory compromise can produce hypoxia (too little oxygen) and hypercapnia (too much carbon dioxide).
Ventilation can be impaired by obstruction, muscle problems, overdose, chest trauma, or allergic airway changes. Gas exchange can be impaired even when air still moves.
A ventilation/perfusion mismatch means air movement and blood flow at the alveoli are not adequately matched. Pulmonary embolism limits blood flow; alveolar edema interferes with exchange.

sections.heading: Consequences
paragraphs: Rising carbon dioxide stimulates increased breathing. If the response is ineffective, acidity rises and oxygen falls. Cells may switch to anaerobic metabolism. Shock likewise reduces tissue oxygen delivery and can cause lactic acid accumulation and organ dysfunction.
bullets: Understanding the mechanism connects abnormal findings to the body system that is failing rather than treating each finding as unrelated.

objectives.objective: Know the terms used to designate the following stages of life: infants, toddlers, preschoolers, school-age children, adolescents (teenagers), early adults, middle adults, and older adults.
objectives.summary: Life-stage labels provide a framework for expected physical development and psychosocial needs; individual patients still require assessment.

sections.heading: Class age bands
bullets: Neonate: birth to 1 month. Infant: 1 month to 1 year.
Toddler: 1–3 years. Preschooler: approximately 3–6 years.
School-age child: 6–12 years.
Adolescent or teenager: 12–18 years.
Early adult: 19–40 years. Middle adult: 41–60 years.
Older adult: 61 years and older.

sections.heading: Use the labels carefully
paragraphs: The boundaries are developmental categories, not sharp changes in physiology on a birthday. Age affects airway anatomy, typical vital signs, communication, independence, and response to illness.
bullets: Young children have smaller, less developed respiratory structures.
School-age children may reason logically but regress when ill or hurt.
Adolescents approach physical maturity while coping with identity, privacy, and peer pressures.
Adult health and conditioning vary greatly; age alone does not describe the patient’s reserve or abilities.

sources.locator: Neonates and Infants; Toddlers and Preschoolers; School-Age Children; Adolescents; Adult stages

objectives.gap: One slide labels preschoolers 4–6 years while the next slide and lecture use 3–6. The study summary uses 3–6, matching the lecture’s preschool discussion.

sections.heading: Preschool age labels
paragraphs: CDC uses ages 3–5 for its preschool parenting guidance. This is a different age grouping from the class lecture’s 3–6 range. An outside definition cannot establish which of the conflicting class slides your instructor intends to test.

outside.note: Keep the class range of 3–6 and ask the instructor to resolve the slide labeled 4–6; developmental age labels vary by source.

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of an infant’s life.
objectives.summary: Infancy involves rapid growth, immature respiratory structures, emerging neurologic abilities, and caregiver attachment.

sections.heading: Physical development
bullets: A neonate commonly weighs 6–8 lb; the head accounts for about 25% of body weight. Growth is about 1 oz per day after the first weeks. Birth weight doubles around 4–6 months and triples by 1 year.
Circulation changes from fetal to independent circulation after birth.

Large tongue, short narrow airway, high anterior larynx, flexible trachea, and large occiput increase obstruction and positioning concerns. Infants younger than 6 months are prone to nasal congestion.

A flexible rib cage and more horizontal ribs contribute to prominent diaphragmatic/abdominal movement. Immature breathing muscles and fewer alveoli leave limited respiratory reserve. Excessive ventilation pressure risks barotrauma.
Posterior fontanelle closes about 3 months; anterior about 9–18 months. A depressed fontanelle can suggest dehydration and a bulging one increased intracranial pressure.
Maternal immunity offers early protection; breast milk supplies antibodies.

sections.heading: Reflexes and milestones
bullets: Moro: startle with arms opening and fingers spreading. Palmar grasp: grasping an object placed in the palm. Rooting: turning toward a touched cheek. Sucking: sucking after lip stimulation.
About 2 months: tracks objects and recognizes familiar faces. About 6 months: sits upright and babbles. About 12 months: walks with minimal assistance. Milestone timing varies.

sections.heading: Psychosocial development
paragraphs: Crying communicates distress. Consistently meeting needs supports trust and secure attachment. Repeated rejection can contribute to anxious-avoidant attachment. Older infants commonly develop separation anxiety; distress when a caregiver leaves is not by itself proof of an attachment disorder.

sources.locator: Neonate growth; pediatric airway; infant reflexes; milestones; fontanelles; attachment

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of a toddler’s and preschooler’s life.
objectives.summary: Toddlers and preschoolers develop independence, language, coordination, and social play while retaining limited respiratory endurance.

sections.heading: Physical development
bullets: Toddlers are 1–3 years; preschoolers are approximately 3–6. Their cardiovascular organization is broadly similar to adults, but normal vital signs differ.
Preschool pulse: 80–140/min; breathing: 20–25/min; systolic pressure: 80–100 mm Hg. These ranges help interpret findings but do not alone prove stability.
Respiratory muscles are not well developed, so prolonged increased effort can lead to fatigue.
The rapid weight gain of infancy levels off. Maternal passive immunity fades and the child’s immune system takes more responsibility.
Neuromuscular coordination improves. The class gives about 28 months as the average completion of toilet training.

sections.heading: Psychosocial development
bullets: Autonomy versus shame and doubt: children seek independence and opportunities to do things themselves. Excessive discouragement can undermine confidence.
Basic language is usually established by about 3 years, allowing better expression of needs.
Children increasingly interact with peers and play games.
Cause and effect begins to be understood around 18–24 months. Children also recognize gender differences through observation of role models.

sections.heading: Patient interaction
paragraphs: Communication should match the child’s actual language and understanding. Growing independence does not mean adult reasoning or adult respiratory reserve.

sources.locator: Toddlers and preschoolers: physiology and psychosocial development

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of a school-age child’s life.
objectives.summary: School-age children become stronger, more coordinated, and more capable of logical thought while developing self-concept and self-esteem.

sections.heading: Physical changes
bullets: School age spans about 6–12 years. Muscles, coordination, organs, and physical abilities continue to mature rapidly.
The class describes yearly growth of about 4 lb and 2.5 inches.
Permanent teeth begin to appear.
Increasing activity in both brain hemispheres accompanies more complex thinking and problem solving.

sections.heading: Reasoning and identity
bullets: Preconventional reasoning: decisions center on avoiding punishment or obtaining what is wanted.
Conventional reasoning: decisions increasingly reflect approval, expectations, and what peers or society consider appropriate.
Postconventional reasoning: decisions reflect a developing personal sense of right and wrong.
Self-concept is the child’s sense of who they are; self-esteem concerns how they feel about themselves.

sections.heading: During illness or injury
paragraphs: School-age children may be independent and logical in ordinary circumstances yet regress toward earlier behaviors when frightened, ill, or injured. Assess the response in context rather than assuming that chronological age guarantees a particular level of cooperation.

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of an adolescent’s life.
objectives.summary: Adolescence combines near-adult physiology and reproductive maturation with strong concerns about independence, identity, privacy, and peer acceptance.

sections.heading: Physical development
bullets: Adolescents are about 12–18 years. Typical pulse is 60–100/min, respirations 12–20/min, and systolic pressure 90–110 mm Hg.
A growth spurt lasts about 2–3 years; the lecture places its completion around 16 in girls and 18 in boys.
Endocrine and reproductive maturation produces secondary sexual characteristics, including pubic and axillary hair, voice changes, and menstruation.

sections.heading: Psychosocial development
bullets: Teens may challenge parents as they seek independence while still needing support.
Privacy, self-consciousness, and identity become important. A patient may want adult treatment while retaining younger needs in a stressful situation.
Peer pressure and risk taking can include smoking, drug use, and unprotected sex; the class describes antisocial behavior peaking around 14–16.
Eating disorders can develop around attempts to control eating or the body.
Personal ethics reflect both family values and experiences with peers. Depression and suicide risk warrant awareness.

sections.heading: Assessment approach
paragraphs: Respect the patient’s developmental concerns and privacy. Adult-like vital signs do not eliminate adolescent psychosocial needs, and apparent confidence does not establish the absence of distress.

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of an early adult’s life.
objectives.summary: Early adulthood commonly has high physical performance and relatively stable vital signs while work, family, and lasting habits become established.

sections.heading: Physical development
bullets: Early adults are 19–40 years. Peak body performance commonly occurs around 19–25.
Pulse is typically 60–100/min, averaging about 70; respirations 12–20/min; systolic pressure 90–120 mm Hg.
After the mid-twenties, gradual aging changes may start even though overall function remains strong.
Health and conditioning vary; individual baseline and current illness or injury still matter.

sections.heading: Psychosocial development
paragraphs: Work, family formation, financial pressures, and establishing a stable place in the world are common concerns. Healthy or unhealthy habits become increasingly established and may shape later health.
bullets: This period is often comparatively stable, but responsibilities and stress can still be substantial.
A patient’s expected age-related reserve should not replace assessment of actual breathing, circulation, and mental status.
Distinguish early-adult work/family priorities from adolescent identity development and later-adult retirement concerns.

sources.locator: Early Adults: physiologic and psychosocial changes

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of a middle adult’s life.
objectives.summary: Middle adulthood brings increasing chronic health risks and sensory changes alongside career, financial, and family responsibilities.

sections.heading: Physical development
bullets: Middle adults are 41–60 years. Typical pulse is 60–100/min, respirations 12–20/min, and systolic pressure 90–140 mm Hg.
Vision and hearing changes become more common.
Cardiovascular disease, cancer risk, diabetes, hypertension, and weight-related concerns become more prominent.
Menopause commonly occurs in the late forties to early fifties.
Exercise and a healthy diet can reduce some aging-related effects and support function.

sections.heading: Psychosocial development
paragraphs: People often focus on career and life goals while adapting to children leaving home. They may face retirement planning, college expenses, and unexpected financial demands. Many care simultaneously for children and aging parents.
bullets: Accumulated physical, emotional, and spiritual resources may help manage these demands.
Stable adult vital-sign ranges do not rule out developing chronic disease.
Communication may require accommodation for hearing or vision changes rather than assuming the patient is inattentive.

sources.locator: Middle Adults: physiologic and psychosocial changes

objectives.objective: Describe the major physical and psychosocial characteristics of an older adult’s life.
objectives.summary: Older adulthood often reduces physiologic reserve and changes sensory function, but aging alone does not establish loss of knowledge, independence, or decision-making ability.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular and respiratory changes
bullets: Arterial plaque and stiffening increase cardiac workload; heart function, cardiac output, blood production, and blood volume may decline.
Lung elasticity and alveolar exchange surface decrease. Breathing muscles weaken and the chest becomes stiffer and more fragile, increasing work and reducing reserve.

Vital capacity may be about half its younger-adult level by age 75. Weaker cough and gag reflexes impair secretion clearance and increase aspiration risk. Infection, airflow limitation, and air trapping become greater concerns.

sections.heading: Other system changes
bullets: Reduced insulin production and declining reproductive hormones alter metabolic and sexual function; sexual interest does not necessarily disappear.
Tooth loss, reduced taste and saliva, lower gastric acid, slower intestinal movement, and less elastic anal sphincters affect digestion and continence. Gallstones become more common.
Kidney blood flow, mass, and filtration decline. The class describes about 50% less filtration between ages 20 and 90 and about 20% less renal mass, impairing waste removal and fluid conservation.
Brain weight may decrease 10–20% by about 80. Slower neural response and peripheral sensation increase fall risk but do not necessarily erase skills or knowledge.
Brain shrinkage can stretch bridging veins, making traumatic subdural bleeding a concern. Vision, pupil response, and especially high-frequency hearing can decline.

sections.heading: Psychosocial needs
paragraphs: Many older adults remain at home and retain strong cognitive function. Some need family, home services, or assisted living. Multiple medications, financial constraints, isolation, depression, and concerns about mortality can affect care.
bullets: Allow time for responses and address hearing or vision barriers before assuming cognitive impairment.
Assess the person’s actual abilities and support needs; aging is highly variable.

sources.locator: Older Adults: system changes and psychosocial changes

objectives.objective: Explain the need and use of the most common patient-moving equipment, the stretcher and backboard.
objectives.summary: Use the device that fits the patient’s condition and route. Rolling reduces carrying when the route permits.

sections.heading: Wheeled stretcher
bullets: The ambulance stretcher or gurney is the most common transport device. It has a main frame, adjustable locking undercarriage, elevating head section, rails, straps, and a fluid-resistant mattress.
Straps secure the patient; rails help prevent rolling off. The adjustable head permits positioning for comfort and breathing needs.
Use wheeled movement when safe rather than carrying a patient a long distance. Wheeled stretchers are generally not taken onto stairs.
Hold the frame securely during loading and secure the stretcher in the ambulance’s clamps. Different loading mechanisms require equipment-specific technique.

sections.heading: Backboard
paragraphs: A backboard is a rigid flat device with handles and strap openings. It can support supine movement, removal from awkward locations, and packaging when indicated for suspected spinal, hip, pelvic, lower-extremity, or multiple injuries.
bullets: A board is a carrying/packaging device; its use depends on patient condition and local protocol.
Choose a stair chair for a conscious patient who can sit; use an appropriate supine device when sitting is unsuitable.

sources.locator: II. Wheeled Ambulance Stretcher; III. Backboards; VII. Stair movement

objectives.objective: Explain the technical skills and general considerations that are required of EMTs during patient packaging and patient handling.
objectives.summary: Patient handling is a technical skill requiring equipment familiarity, planning, coordinated teamwork, and repeated practice.

sections.heading: Before movement
bullets: Determine whether scene danger or patient condition requires emergency or urgent movement, or whether a deliberate nonurgent plan is possible.
Assess patient position, injuries, weight, ability to sit, available space, route, and equipment limitations.
Arrange enough people before the lift and assign their positions.
Explain the move to the patient when possible and protect comfort and privacy.
Know each device’s advantages, limitations, controls, and securing features before using it.

sections.heading: Team execution
paragraphs: The team leader describes the sequence and uses preparatory commands and a countdown so everyone moves together. Patient movement should be orderly and unhurried whenever the circumstances allow.
bullets: Use proper body mechanics and maintain physical fitness.
Secure and support the patient to prevent falls and further injury.
Reassess whether the planned position and technique remain appropriate as circumstances change.
A technically correct device choice still requires a safe route and enough personnel.

sources.locator: IV. Moving and Positioning; VIII. Directions and Commands; XVII. Personnel Considerations

objectives.objective: Define the term body mechanics.
objectives.summary: Body mechanics is the relationship between anatomic structures and the physical forces involved in lifting, moving, and carrying.

sections.heading: Alignment and force
paragraphs: When upright, the weight-bearing vertebrae align above the sacrum, the spine’s mechanical and weight-bearing base. Maintaining alignment reduces strain. Leaning forward, or keeping a straight back while bending far forward at the hips, can still injure the back.
bullets: Balance the feet and center of gravity.
Keep the torso upright during lifting and lower by bending the legs.
Keep the load close; avoid outstretched arms and sideways leverage.
Use leg extension to lift rather than straightening a bent back.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The same weight can place very different force on the back depending on posture and distance from the body. A strong grip cannot compensate for poor spinal alignment, inadequate personnel, or unsafe reach.

objectives.objective: Discuss how following proper patient lifting and moving techniques can help prevent work-related injuries.
objectives.summary: Safe lifting limits strain by keeping the load close, the spine aligned, and the lifting force in the legs.

sections.heading: Power lift sequence
bullets: Place feet about shoulder width—approximately 15 inches apart—and balance weight on the balls of the feet.
Keep the back upright while bending the legs to lower the body.
Grip the load securely near the body and adjust foot position before lifting.
Straighten the properly positioned, flexed legs to rise; bring the arms toward waist height without leaning or twisting.

sections.heading: Prevent injury
bullets: Prefer rolling devices to carrying where possible.
Use sufficient personnel and coordinate the start, direction, and finish of the move.
Use powered or specialized equipment when needed; check its rated capacity.
Maintain physical conditioning and practice techniques before field use.
Stop safely and obtain assistance if a provider develops sharp pain or cannot continue securely.

sections.heading: Core distinction
paragraphs: A straight back is only part of safe technique. A torso bent forward at the hips can still impose unsafe leverage. The load, alignment, route, and available help must all fit the planned movement.

sources.locator: IV–V. Moving and Body Mechanics; VII. Safe Lifting and Carrying
Stair-chair carry: sudden sharp lower-back pain and additional lifting assistance

objectives.objective: Identify how to avoid common mistakes when lifting and carrying a patient.
objectives.summary: Avoid overreaching, twisting, lifting with outstretched arms, and treating a straight but forward-bent back as safe.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and corrections
bullets: Forward lean while lifting: lower with the legs and keep the upper body upright.
Load held far away: bring it close rather than lifting with extended arms.
Sideways leverage or twisting: maintain alignment and coordinate the move instead of rotating under load.
Unbalanced stance: adjust feet before lifting.
Overreaching across a bed: kneel on the bed to stay within a safe reach.

sections.heading: Reaching and pulling sequence
paragraphs: For a body drag, tighten abdominal muscles to maintain the back’s slight curve, kneel, and reach no more than about 15–20 inches ahead. Pull in controlled increments, stop when the hands reach the torso, then move back and repeat. For a bed drag, use the sheet or blanket beneath the patient.
bullets: Move closer or reposition instead of increasing reach.
For a stretcher-to-bed transfer, the stretcher is level with or slightly above the bed; providers kneel on the bed and move in increments.
When log rolling, kneel close, maintain a straight back, and pull toward the thighs so they help prevent over-rolling.

sources.locator: V. Lifting technique; VI. Safe Reaching and Pulling

objectives.objective: Explain the power grip and sheet or blanket methods for lifting a patient.
objectives.summary: A power grip maximizes secure hand support; a sheet or blanket spreads support during a coordinated transfer.

sections.heading: Power grip
bullets: Use palms upward with thumbs extended outward.
Keep hands about 10 inches apart where the device permits.
Curl fingers and thumbs firmly over the handle, with fingers at the same angle.
Support the handle fully on the curved palm rather than hanging it from the fingertips.
When directly gripping a patient, choose support points and a hold that will not slip.

sections.heading: Sheet or blanket transfer
paragraphs: With two or more rescuers, use the sheet or blanket beneath a supine patient to transfer from bed to stretcher. Plan the move, position the devices close enough for safe reach, and move together on commands.
bullets: Use the supporting sheet, not clothing traction, for a planned bed transfer.
Kneel on the bed if needed to avoid excessive reaching; pull in short increments and reposition.
The direct carry is a different technique in which rescuers support the patient directly rather than transferring with a sheet.

sources.locator: V. Power grip; VI.C–D. Bed and hospital transfers; XI.D. Draw sheet method

objectives.objective: Explain the general considerations required of EMTs to safely move patients without causing the patient further harm and while protecting themselves from injury.
objectives.summary: Safe movement requires matching patient needs, personnel capability, equipment capacity, route, and team coordination.

sections.heading: Assess before lifting
bullets: Estimate weight and identify injuries or conditions that affect position and support.
Confirm equipment capacity and decide whether specialized resources are needed.
Check space for a safe stance, obstacles, stairs, and ambulance access.
Ask whether you are physically able to perform the move and whether more personnel are needed.
Use rolling movement whenever practical.

sections.heading: Personnel and weight
bullets: Use four providers whenever possible for carrying. The class says not to lift a patient over 250 lb with fewer than four providers.
Patients over about 350 lb generally require bariatric techniques, equipment, and resources.
More weight rests toward the head half of a stretcher/backboard. Distribute personnel accordingly.
A diamond carry has one at the head, one at the feet, and one on each side of the torso. A one-handed carry uses four or more providers facing forward.

sections.heading: Patient protection
paragraphs: Secure the patient, preserve indicated spinal restriction, and communicate every step. Device capacity does not establish that the crew can safely lift that weight. Stop and revise the plan if safe mechanics or grip cannot be maintained.

sources.locator: VII. Safe Lifting and Carrying; VIII. Commands; XVII. Personnel Considerations

objectives.objective: Explain how to carry patients safely on stairs, including the selection of appropriate equipment to aid in the process.
objectives.summary: Stair equipment depends on whether the patient can safely sit or must remain supine and supported.

sections.heading: Seated patient
paragraphs: Use a stair chair for a conscious patient whose condition permits sitting. Secure its adjustable straps and use its head/foot handles as a coordinated team. It can roll on level surfaces and brings the patient to the prepared ambulance stretcher.
bullets: Confirm the route and assign positions before moving.
Follow equipment-specific instructions and communicate the start and each change in movement.
Do not substitute sitting for required supine support merely because a stair chair is convenient.

sections.heading: Supine patient
paragraphs: For an unresponsive patient, a patient who must remain supine, or one requiring immobilization, the class describes backboard movement down stairs to a prepared stretcher.
bullets: Place the strongest providers at the head and foot ends; the taller provider is at the foot end.
Maintain secure patient packaging and controlled, coordinated movement.
Use the wheeled stretcher for the level portion when the route permits.
If a provider experiences sharp pain, coordinate a safe stop and request assistance.

sources.locator: VII.E–F. Stair chair and backboard stair movement
Stair-chair carry: sudden sharp lower-back pain and additional lifting assistance

objectives.objective: Describe specific situations in which an emergency move may be necessary to move a patient; include how each one is performed.
objectives.summary: An emergency move removes a patient from immediate danger or a location that prevents immediate assessment or care.

sections.heading: Indications
paragraphs: Use emergency movement when the scene poses an uncontrolled threat such as advancing fire, or the patient’s location prevents necessary immediate access or care. Prioritize reaching safety while minimizing avoidable spinal movement.

sections.heading: Emergency drag methods
bullets: Clothes drag: grasp clothing around the neck and shoulders and pull.
Blanket drag: place the patient on a blanket, coat, or similar material and pull it.
Arm drag: extend the arms on the ground beyond the head, grasp the wrists, and drag.
Arm-to-arm drag: reach under the shoulders through the armpits, grasp your opposite wrist, and move backward.

sections.heading: Alone at a vehicle
bullets: First clear the legs from the pedals.
Turn the patient so the back faces the open door.
Reach under the shoulders through the armpits and support the head against your body.
Once the legs and feet clear the vehicle, drag the patient rapidly to safety.

sections.heading: Key distinction
paragraphs: Do not delay escape from uncontrolled danger for a complete nonurgent packaging process. These techniques answer an immediate threat; they are not preferred routine transfers at a safe, stable scene.

objectives.objective: Describe specific situations in which an urgent move or rapid extrication may be necessary to move a patient; include how each one is performed.
objectives.summary: Urgent movement is needed when the patient’s condition requires prompt access or transport. Rapid extrication is reserved for a specific urgent need.

sections.heading: Urgent conditions
bullets: Altered consciousness, inadequate ventilation, or shock can require an urgent move.

Rapid vehicle extrication may be needed for an unsafe scene, fire/explosive hazard, inability to assess the seated patient, an immediate intervention requiring a supine position, a life-threatening condition needing transport, or blocked access to another seriously injured patient.

sections.heading: Rapid extrication approach
paragraphs: Use a coordinated team to move the seated patient from the vehicle to a supine carrying/transport position, supporting the patient and limiting unnecessary spinal movement. The class describes transfer to a backboard in one minute or less; whether a backboard is used depends on local protocol. Move away from the hazard and begin lifesaving care.
bullets: Assess other available options before choosing rapid extrication.
The speed increases the risk of aggravating a spinal injury.
Urgency changes the timing of movement; it does not eliminate teamwork or support.
A stable seated patient who can be assessed and treated in place does not require rapid extrication merely because a collision occurred.

sources.locator: X. Urgent Moves; rapid extrication indications

objectives.gap: The supplied lecture identifies indications and the overall transfer but refers to a separate skill drill for the full hands-on team sequence. Those detailed drill steps are not included.

sections.heading: Traditional rapid vehicle-extrication sequence
paragraphs: This sequence describes a traditional team technique in the historical NHTSA curriculum. It supplies the missing overview, but is not a current local skill checklist. Equipment, spinal-motion restrictions, and the safest extrication method must follow current training and protocol.
bullets: Assign one rescuer to manual head and neck support. A second supports the torso and applies the indicated cervical device; a third prepares the transfer board and frees the legs.
Rotate the torso and legs together in short, coordinated movements until the back faces the open door. Transfer head support between rescuers without leaving the head unsupported.
Place the board next to the buttocks, support its outer end, and lower the patient onto it. Slide the patient into position using coordinated movements, then continue urgent care and transport.

outside.note: Confirm the current classroom team sequence and equipment. The historical source does not establish current local practice.

objectives.objective: Describe specific situations in which a nonurgent move may be necessary to move a patient; include how each one is performed.
objectives.summary: Nonurgent movement is used when both the patient and scene are stable, allowing careful planning and selection of an appropriate transfer.

sections.heading: Lifting and carrying
bullets: Direct ground lift: for a supine patient without suspected spinal injury who needs carrying to a stretcher; rescuers stand side by side and lift together.
Extremity lift: for a supine or seated patient without suspected spinal or extremity injury, particularly in a small space; one rescuer works at the head, another at the feet, using commands.

sections.heading: Transfer methods
bullets: Direct carry: two or more rescuers directly support a supine patient from bed to stretcher.
Draw sheet: two or more rescuers transfer using the sheet or blanket beneath the patient.
Scoop stretcher: place separated halves around each side, reconnect them, secure the patient, and lift with two or more rescuers. Both sides must be accessible.
Log roll or slide: place the patient onto an appropriate backboard, secure, then lift and carry to the prepared stretcher.

sections.heading: Assisted stand-and-pivot
paragraphs: When appropriate, help the patient sit at the bed edge with legs over the side. Position the stretcher near the bed, assist standing and rotation onto its center, then lift the legs while a partner lowers the torso.
bullets: Choose by injuries, ability to cooperate, space, and required position.
Coordinate even a routine transfer; stability is not permission to use unsafe reach or grip.

objectives.objective: Explain the special considerations and guidelines related to moving and transporting geriatric patients.
objectives.summary: Older patients may need adapted packaging because brittle bones, skeletal rigidity, and spinal curvature can make standard flat devices uncomfortable or harmful.

sections.heading: Assessment and packaging
bullets: Check whether the patient can tolerate lying supine and whether curvature prevents safe support on a rigid board or scoop stretcher.
Do not force the patient into a flat position without considering these structural changes.
Consider a geriatric-appropriate device such as a vacuum mattress, which molds around the body while providing support.
Explain movement and handling, protect dignity, and use coordinated, controlled transfer.

sections.heading: Device selection
paragraphs: A vacuum mattress is shaped around the patient and stiffens when its air is removed. It can offer immobilization, comfort, and thermal insulation. The goal is adequate support that accommodates the actual patient’s shape and condition.
bullets: Chronological age does not by itself determine which device is required.
Assess suspected injury and available equipment as well as age-related changes.
A familiar rigid device is not automatically appropriate if it increases pain or risks further injury.

sources.locator: XII. Geriatrics; XIV.F. Vacuum mattresses; Enhancements: patient privacy

objectives.objective: Define the term bariatrics.
objectives.summary: Bariatrics is the management, prevention, or control of obesity and associated diseases.

sections.heading: Meaning and EMS relevance
paragraphs: The term describes a field concerned with obesity, not simply a piece of lifting equipment. In EMS, bariatric care includes selecting safe movement resources for patients whose size or weight exceeds ordinary equipment or crew capability.
bullets: Patient needs and provider safety both matter.
A bariatric stretcher commonly has a wider patient surface, wider wheelbase, and greater rated capacity.
The equipment’s higher capacity does not remove the force imposed on providers during a manual lift.
Respectful planning should happen before lifting rather than after a failed attempt.

sections.heading: Distinguish the term
paragraphs: Geriatric care concerns older adults; bariatric care concerns obesity and associated disease. An older patient may also need bariatric resources, but the terms describe different issues.

objectives.objective: Discuss the guidelines for lifting and moving bariatric patients.
objectives.summary: Bariatric movement requires equipment suited to the patient and enough personnel or mechanical assistance for the entire route and loading process.

sections.heading: Plan before movement
bullets: Estimate weight and compare it with every device’s rated limit.
Check room, doorway width, stairs, turning space, and ambulance loading arrangements.
Request enough personnel and specialized bariatric equipment before trying the lift.
Use at least four providers for a patient over 250 lb; the class notes specialized bariatric resources generally become necessary over 350 lb.
A wider surface and wheelbase improve accommodation and stability, while powered movement can reduce manual force.

sections.heading: Capacity versus crew safety
paragraphs: A stretcher rating states what the equipment can support, not what the crew can safely lift. Back injuries are a major occupational burden, and stronger equipment alone does not resolve that risk.
bullets: Use rolling movement where possible.
Maintain coordinated commands, secure patient support, and proper body mechanics.
Reassess the plan if there is insufficient room for a safe stance or grip.
Protect the patient’s dignity while discussing and arranging resources.

sources.locator: VII.C. Patient weight; XIII. Bariatrics; XIV.A–B. Specialized stretchers; XVII. Personnel Considerations

objectives.objective: Explain the need and use for additional patient-moving equipment (specialized); include examples.
objectives.summary: Specialized equipment solves particular access, positioning, size, or support needs; choose it according to the patient and environment.

sections.heading: Equipment and purpose
bullets: Bariatric stretcher: larger surface, wider wheelbase, and higher capacity for large patients.
Pneumatic or electronic-powered stretcher: raises and lowers the undercarriage using air or battery power, reducing manual effort.
Portable/folding stretcher: lighter rigid-frame/fabric device for difficult-to-reach areas.
Flexible stretcher: rolls into a small package and conforms around the patient for confined-space removal.
Short backboard or vest device such as a KED: supports the head, neck, and torso of a seated patient with suspected spinal injury during packaging.
Vacuum mattress: molds around the body after air removal, providing support, comfort, and insulation, especially useful for some older or pediatric patients.
Basket stretcher: rigid device for uneven remote terrain and some rope/water rescue settings; indicated spinal support is secured within it.
Scoop stretcher: separates into pieces placed around a supine patient, then reconnects for lifting. Both sides must be accessible.
Neonatal isolette: provides a warm, clean environment with moistened air and protects against drafts, noise, infection, and excess handling.

sections.heading: Use requirements
paragraphs: A specialized device still needs appropriate patient securing, trained handling, rated-capacity checks, and correct ambulance attachment. Equipment familiarity and local procedures govern its safe use.

objectives.objective: Explain the importance of decontaminating equipment in the prevention of disease transmission.
objectives.summary: Decontaminate patient-moving equipment after use to prevent disease transmission to patients and responders.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: A device can carry infectious material from one encounter into the next. Cleaning and disinfection protect the provider who used it, later crews, and future patients. A fluid-resistant stretcher mattress facilitates cleaning, but the whole required equipment process must still be completed.
bullets: Follow local standard operating procedures for disinfecting equipment.
Include equipment exposed during the encounter according to those procedures, rather than assuming replacement of one component completes the process.
Visible cleanliness alone does not establish readiness for another patient.
Secure storage is not a substitute for decontamination.

sections.heading: Ready for reuse
paragraphs: The practical endpoint is completion of the required post-use process before the device is used again. The class does not specify a universal disinfectant or contact time; use the local procedure for those details.

objectives.objective: Describe proper positioning of unresponsive patients without suspected spine injury; patients with chest pain, discomfort, or difficulty breathing; patients with suspected spine injury; pregnant patients with hypotension; and patients who are nauseated or vomiting.
objectives.summary: Positioning follows the complaint, airway needs, circulation, and suspected injuries rather than one position for every patient.

sections.heading: Match position to condition
bullets: Unresponsive, with no suspected spinal, hip, or pelvic injury: recovery position on the side.
Chest pain, discomfort, or respiratory distress without suspected injury: position of comfort, typically Fowler or semi-Fowler.
Shock: supine packaging and positioning.
Suspected spinal injury: maintain appropriate spinal restriction and support; do not freely reposition for comfort without considering the injury.
Late pregnancy with hypotension or discomfort while supine: left-side positioning and transport to reduce pressure on major vessels.
Nausea or vomiting: position of comfort with attention to airway protection.

sections.heading: Reassess the position
paragraphs: The same complaint may coexist with another problem that changes the plan. For example, upright comfort is not the default for a patient in shock, and the routine recovery position is not the default when spinal, hip, or pelvic injury is suspected.
bullets: Maintain securing straps and necessary support during transport.
Continue watching breathing, perfusion, and tolerance after any position change.

objectives.objective: Identify the components of the patient assessment process.
objectives.summary: Patient assessment has five connected parts. Its order can change when the patient needs immediate treatment.

sections.heading: Introduction · Assessment phases
bullets: Scene size-up: evaluate safety, standard precautions, mechanism of injury or nature of illness, number of patients, and additional resources before approaching.
Primary assessment: form a general impression, assess responsiveness and airway, breathing, and circulation, identify and treat life threats, and decide transport priority.
History taking: investigate the chief complaint and collect relevant background using OPQRST and SAMPLE.
Secondary assessment: perform a focused or systematic physical examination and obtain vital signs to find additional problems.
Reassessment: repeat the primary assessment, compare vital signs, revisit the complaint, and check interventions.

A sign is observable or measurable, such as bleeding or a blood pressure reading. A symptom is what the patient reports feeling, such as nausea or pain. Combine findings rather than relying on one clue.

objectives.objective: Explain how the different causes and presentations of emergencies will affect how EMTs perform each step of the patient assessment process.
objectives.summary: Use the assessment framework flexibly. The patient’s immediate needs determine which action takes priority.

sections.heading: Introduction · Flexible sequence
bullets: Scene safety comes first. An unsafe environment may require waiting for specialized resources before patient contact.
For a patient showing signs of life, assess airway, breathing, and circulation while treating problems as they are found.
For a lifeless patient with absent normal breathing or only agonal gasps, evaluate circulation promptly and begin compressions if pulseless; this is the CAB approach.
Uncontrolled external hemorrhage requires immediate bleeding control rather than waiting for the rest of the assessment.
A stable patient with an isolated complaint may receive a focused examination on scene. A critical patient may need transport while further assessment continues in the ambulance.
Medical and traumatic problems can coexist. A fall may cause injuries but have begun because of a medical problem. Keep revising your working impression as new information appears.

objectives.objective: Discuss some of the possible environmental, chemical, and biologic hazards that may be present at an emergency scene, ways to recognize them, and precautions to protect personal safety.
objectives.summary: Recognize scene hazards before contact and keep checking throughout the call. Several people with similar symptoms may signal a shared environmental danger.

sections.heading: Scene Size-up · Scene safety
bullets: Environmental hazards include extreme weather, darkness, uneven terrain, water, and traffic. They can affect access, transport, patient condition, and equipment.
Physical hazards include sharp metal, broken glass, and slip or fall risks. Electrical hazards include downed lines; fire and explosion hazards require specialized assistance.

Chemical hazards include hazardous materials and unknown substances. Multiple people with headache, nausea, or dizziness in one setting should raise concern for carbon monoxide or another shared exposure.
Biologic exposure includes blood, body fluids, nonintact skin, mucous membranes, and contaminated equipment. Take standard precautions and match PPE to likely exposure.

Do not enter a dangerous scene beyond your training. Request fire, hazardous-materials, law-enforcement, or utility support as appropriate. Protect bystanders from becoming additional patients when it is safe to do so.
Dispatch information is a starting point; observations at arrival may reveal a different situation.

sources.locator: II. Scene Size-up · Hazards and standard precautions
