objectives.objective: Discuss the steps EMTs should take to survey a scene for signs of violence and to protect themselves and bystanders from real or potential danger.
objectives.summary: Survey for threats of violence, use a calm approach, and withdraw when a scene is unsafe. Scene security can change after arrival.

sections.heading: Scene Size-up · Violence
bullets: Use dispatch information and your observations to identify potential danger before approaching the patient.
Watch for violent patients, distraught or aggressive relatives, angry bystanders, gangs, and unruly crowds. Do not assume a scene is safe because the original call sounded routine.
Avoid arguing, accusing people, or matching their anger. Speak calmly and reassuringly and keep your approach gentle.
Do not corner an intoxicated patient or make the person feel threatened with no way out. Impaired judgment increases the risk of confrontation.
If the scene is unsafe or hostility escalates, retreat and wait for law enforcement to secure it. Patient care resumes when you can operate safely.
When appropriate and safe, guide bystanders away from hazards. Maintain situational awareness for the whole call, including changes in crowd behavior or new people arriving.

sources.locator: II. Scene Size-up · Violence; IV. History Taking · Anger and intoxication

objectives.objective: Describe how to determine the mechanism of injury (MOI) or nature of illness (NOI) at an emergency and the importance of differentiating trauma patients from medical patients.
objectives.summary: MOI describes the physical forces causing injury; NOI describes the medical problem. Both guide preparation without replacing assessment.

sections.heading: Scene Size-up · Mechanism of injury and nature of illness
bullets: Trauma results from an external force, such as the body striking an object in a fall or an object striking the body in a crash.
Blunt trauma may cause serious hidden injury without an open wound. Penetrating trauma breaks the skin and may injure deeper organs or blood vessels even when the entrance wound is small.
Determine MOI from the scene, the event description, patient and witness accounts, and visible damage or injuries.
Determine NOI by asking about the chief complaint, observing the patient, and gathering clues from relatives, bystanders, medications, and surroundings.
Medical problems include chest pain, breathing difficulty, and altered mental status. Trauma and illness can occur together; investigate a possible medical cause of a traumatic event.
MOI and NOI help anticipate equipment, spinal concerns, transport urgency, and areas to examine. They do not prove a diagnosis or exclude a problem that does not fit the initial story.

sources.locator: Blunt versus penetrating trauma; medical cause of a fall

objectives.objective: List the minimum standard precautions that should be followed and personal protective equipment (PPE) that should be worn at an emergency scene, including examples of when additional precautions would be appropriate.
objectives.summary: Take standard precautions before patient contact. Gloves are the minimum; add protection according to the task and exposure risk.

sections.heading: Scene Size-up · Standard precautions
bullets: Assume blood, body fluids other than sweat, nonintact skin, and mucous membranes may transmit infection. You cannot reliably identify an infectious patient by appearance.
Put gloves on before touching the patient. Protection should be initiated before leaving the EMS vehicle and adjusted as the situation develops.
Use eye protection and a mask when splashes or airway secretions may reach the face. Add a gown when clothing or exposed skin may be contaminated.

Increase facial and clothing protection when the task may expose you to blood, vomit, or other secretions. Heavy bleeding or vomiting can change the exposure risk after an initially routine assessment.
Account for contaminated objects and equipment as well as direct contact with the patient. A routine call may become a higher-exposure situation if heavy bleeding or vomiting begins.
Choose PPE for the work actually being performed; standard precautions apply to every patient interaction.

objectives.objective: Explain why it is important for EMTs to identify the total number of patients at an emergency scene and how this evaluation relates to determining the need for additional or specialized resources, implementation of the incident command system (ICS), and triage.
objectives.summary: Count all patients early so resources, treatment, and transport can be organized before the scene overwhelms one crew.

sections.heading: Scene Size-up · Patient count and resources
bullets: Accurately identify the total number of patients during scene size-up. Do not focus so closely on the first patient that others are missed.
For multiple patients, use the incident command system, determine the patient count, and begin triage.
Triage sorts patients by the severity of their condition to establish treatment and transport priorities.
Ask three resource questions: Is the scene dangerous? How many patients are present? Do we have the personnel, equipment, and level of care their conditions require?
Request additional ambulances when patient numbers exceed your capacity. ALS or air medical support may be needed for patient care or transport.
Fire and rescue resources may handle hazardous materials, extrication, wilderness, high-angle, or water rescue. Law enforcement addresses violence and scene security.
Recognizing needs early helps avoid delays. Patient count and resource needs should be updated if the incident changes.

sources.locator: Scene Size-up · Patient count and resources

objectives.objective: Describe the principal goals of the primary assessment process, including how to identify and treat life threats and determine if immediate transport is required.
objectives.summary: The primary assessment finds and begins treatment of immediate or imminent life threats and establishes transport priority.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Purpose and priorities
bullets: Form a general impression, assess the level of consciousness, and examine airway, breathing, and circulation.
Scan immediately for uncontrolled external bleeding and control severe hemorrhage when identified.
Ensure airway patency; clear obstruction and open the airway as needed. Determine whether breathing is present and adequate, and provide oxygen or ventilation support according to the findings.
Evaluate pulse, skin, and signs of perfusion. An unresponsive pulseless patient requires CPR.
Life threats include airway obstruction, respiratory failure or arrest, shock, severe bleeding, and cardiac arrest. Treat problems immediately instead of finishing a checklist first.

Determine whether the patient is stable, potentially unstable, or unstable. High-priority findings require prompt transport; continuing history and secondary examination must not delay needed definitive care.
Reassess after interventions because an initial correction may fail or another life threat may emerge.

objectives.objective: Explain the process of forming a general impression of a patient as part of primary assessment and the reasons why this step is critical to patient management.
objectives.summary: The general impression is the first overall judgment of how sick or injured the patient appears. It guides urgency before the detailed examination.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · General impression
bullets: As you approach, note approximate age, overall appearance, apparent distress, position, and whether the patient is moving or still.
Make sure the patient sees you coming when possible. Introduce yourself, use the patient’s name, and avoid standing over the person unnecessarily.
Ask what is wrong. The response can reveal mental status, airway patency, respiratory difficulty, and clues to circulation.
Observe whether the patient appears stable, stable but potentially unstable, or unstable. This judgment helps determine the next assessment actions and priority of care.
A patient who speaks only a few words, looks pale, or cannot respond normally needs immediate attention to the relevant life threats.

The general impression is provisional. Combine it with examination and vital signs, and revise it when findings change. Treat obvious life-threatening problems during this first contact rather than postponing care until the impression is complete.

objectives.objective: Explain the importance of assessing a patient’s level of consciousness (LOC) to determine altered mental status, and include examples of different methods used to assess alertness, responsiveness, and orientation.
objectives.summary: Responsiveness, orientation, and GCS describe different aspects of mental status. Compare findings with the patient’s usual baseline.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Mental status
bullets: AVPU: Alert; responds to Verbal stimuli; responds to Painful stimuli; Unresponsive. Record what produces a response rather than assuming that speaking automatically means fully alert.
Orientation checks person, place, time, and event: name, current location, approximate date, and what happened. A deviation from full orientation or the usual baseline is altered mental status.
GCS adds eye, verbal, and motor scores. Eyes: spontaneous 4, sound 3, pressure 2, none 1. Verbal: oriented 5, confused 4, words 3, sounds 2, none 1.
GCS motor: obeys commands 6, localizes 5, normal flexion/withdrawal 4, abnormal flexion 3, extension 2, none 1. Sum all three components; total range is 3–15.
Localization means moving toward the stimulus; withdrawal means moving away. GCS is not interchangeable with A&O.
Altered status may reflect poor perfusion, hypoxia, injury, medication, drugs, alcohol, or poisoning. Assess and treat underlying life threats.

sources.locator: III. Primary Assessment · LOC, AVPU, and orientation

objectives.objective: Describe the assessment of airway status in patients who are both responsive and unresponsive, including examples of possible signs and causes of airway obstruction in each case as well as the appropriate EMT response.
objectives.summary: Assess airway patency immediately and correct obstruction before continuing. A patient who can talk or cry has airflow, but abnormal sounds require attention.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Airway
bullets: Responsive patients: listen to speech or crying. Inability to speak or cry may indicate severe obstruction. Look for visible injury, blood, secretions, or material blocking the airway.
Unresponsive patients: assess airway patency immediately. Relaxation of the tongue can obstruct the airway.
Snoring, bubbling, gurgling, crowing, and stridor are abnormal airway sounds. Extremely shallow or absent breathing may accompany obstruction.
If trauma is possible, open the airway with a jaw-thrust. If this fails to open it, use the head tilt–chin lift; an open airway remains essential.
Use head tilt–chin lift when spinal trauma is not suspected. Suction fluids or secretions when needed and remove only visible obstructing material.
If airway difficulty or abnormal breathing appears later, reassess the airway immediately. An airway that was patent initially may become obstructed during care or transport.

objectives.objective: Describe the assessment of a patient’s breathing status, including the key information EMTs must obtain during this process and the care required for patients who have both adequate and inadequate breathing.
objectives.summary: Assess whether breathing is present, whether air movement is adequate, and whether oxygenation is adequate. These are related but separate questions.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Breathing
bullets: Observe rate, rhythm, depth, chest rise, and effort. Shallow chest movement indicates reduced tidal volume; rate alone does not establish adequate ventilation.
Look for retractions, accessory-muscle use, nasal flaring, labored breathing, tripod or sniffing posture, and difficulty speaking more than a few words.
If breathing is adequate but the patient remains hypoxic, administer supplemental oxygen. The patient assessment material gives an oxygen saturation goal of about 94–99% for most patients.
If breathing is absent, too slow, or too shallow to provide adequate air exchange, provide positive-pressure ventilation with an appropriate adjunct.

The material advises considering assisted ventilation when respirations exceed 28/min, are below 8/min, or are too shallow. Interpret these findings with the whole presentation rather than rate alone.
Reevaluate the airway immediately if breathing deteriorates after the primary assessment. Continue checking the response to oxygen or assisted ventilation.

objectives.objective: List the signs of respiratory distress and respiratory failure.
objectives.summary: Respiratory distress is increased work of breathing. Respiratory failure means oxygenation or ventilation is no longer meeting the body’s needs.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Respiratory distress and failure
bullets: Distress signs include increased rate and effort, retractions, accessory-muscle use, nasal flaring, labored breathing, tripod posture, and speaking only two or three words at a time.
Watch chest movement and tidal volume. A patient can breathe rapidly while moving too little air with each breath.
Failure is suggested by inadequate air movement, shallow or slowing respirations, exhaustion, deteriorating mental status, and signs of poor oxygenation such as cyanosis.
Distress can progress to failure as the patient tires. Do not assume that less visible effort means improvement if chest rise or alertness is worsening.
Respiratory arrest is the eventual result if failure is not corrected. Provide ventilation support when breathing becomes inadequate.
Agonal gasps are not effective breathing. Abnormal breath patterns and unequal chest expansion also demand prompt assessment and treatment.

sources.locator: III. Primary Assessment · Breathing and respiratory failure

objectives.objective: Describe the assessment of a patient’s circulatory status, including the different methods for obtaining a pulse and appropriate management depending on the patient’s status.
objectives.summary: Circulation assessment combines mental status, pulse, skin findings, and bleeding. A pulse alone does not establish adequate perfusion.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Circulation
bullets: Palpate the pulse to determine whether it is present. In a responsive patient older than 1 year, use the radial artery at the wrist.
In an unresponsive patient older than 1 year, use the carotid artery in the neck. In an infant younger than 1 year, use the brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm.
Assess rate, rhythm, and quality as care continues. A weak or abnormal pulse must be interpreted with mental status, skin, and other findings.
If an unresponsive patient has no palpable pulse, begin CPR. Severe external bleeding needs immediate control.
Skin color, temperature, moisture, and capillary refill help assess perfusion. Pale, cool, moist skin or altered mental status can indicate poor circulation.
Do not wait for low blood pressure to recognize shock. The cardiovascular material identifies decreased pressure as a late sign; trends and the complete examination matter.

objectives.objective: Explain the variations required to obtain a pulse in infant and child patients compared with adult patients.
objectives.summary: Choose the pulse site by age and responsiveness. Infants use a different primary site from older children and adults.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Pediatric pulse assessment
bullets: For an infant younger than 1 year, palpate the brachial pulse along the medial, or inside, portion of the upper arm.
For a responsive child older than 1 year, palpate the radial pulse at the wrist, as you would in a responsive adult.
For an unresponsive child older than 1 year, assess the carotid pulse in the neck, as you would in an unresponsive adult.
The change is based on age and patient status, not simply on calling someone a pediatric patient. A responsive child and an unresponsive child may require different sites.
Assess whether a pulse is present and then consider its rate, quality, and rhythm with skin findings and mental status.

A pulseless, unresponsive patient requires immediate resuscitative care. Do not use the absence of a difficult-to-find peripheral pulse alone as a substitute for the appropriate central pulse assessment.

objectives.objective: Describe the assessment of a patient’s skin color, temperature, and condition, including examples of both normal and abnormal findings and the information this provides related to the patient’s status.
objectives.summary: Skin provides clues to perfusion and oxygenation. Evaluate color, temperature, moisture, and capillary refill together with the rest of the assessment.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Skin and capillary refill
bullets: Normal skin is generally warm and dry, with color appropriate to the patient’s baseline.
Poor peripheral circulation can produce pale, white, ashen, or gray skin. Bluish discoloration suggests inadequate oxygen saturation. Flushing may accompany abnormal circulation or other conditions.
Hot, cool, cold, or clammy skin is abnormal. Wet or moist skin and excessively dry, hot skin warrant further assessment.
Assess capillary refill by pressing a fingernail or fingertip until it blanches, releasing pressure, and observing return of normal color. The slides give a normal return within 2 seconds.
Capillary refill is particularly used in pediatric assessment, but it is only one perfusion finding. Interpret it with pulse, mental status, skin temperature, and the environment.
Describe observed findings clearly and compare with the patient’s baseline. Skin findings help recognize deterioration but do not by themselves identify the exact cause.

objectives.objective: Discuss the process of assessing for and methods for controlling external bleeding.
objectives.summary: Look early for uncontrolled external bleeding and treat it immediately. Severe hemorrhage can take priority over the usual ABC order.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · External bleeding
bullets: Scan the patient for visible severe bleeding during first contact, using gloves and other PPE appropriate to the exposure.
Expose the area enough to identify the source. Bleeding from a large vein may flow steadily; arterial bleeding may spurt.
Apply direct pressure to control external bleeding. Do not postpone control while obtaining supplies or completing unrelated assessment steps.
If direct pressure is not quickly successful, or there is obvious arterial hemorrhage from an extremity, apply a tourniquet as described in the course material.
Assess circulation and signs of poor perfusion while managing the bleeding. The amount of visible blood and the patient’s overall condition both affect urgency.
Continue checking that bleeding remains controlled after movement, packaging, and transport. Reassessment includes the effectiveness of every intervention.
A patient with uncontrolled bleeding is high priority and needs prompt transport while immediate treatment continues.

objectives.objective: Discuss the steps used to identify and subsequently treat life-threatening conditions that endanger a patient during an emergency.
objectives.summary: Identify life threats quickly, treat them as they are discovered, and arrange prompt transport for problems requiring care beyond the EMT level.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Identifying and treating life threats
bullets: Begin with scene safety and a general impression, then assess responsiveness and scan for uncontrolled hemorrhage.
Assess airway patency and correct obstruction. Assess breathing and provide oxygen for hypoxia or positive-pressure ventilation for absent or inadequate breathing.
Assess circulation using pulse, mental status, and skin. Start CPR when the patient is unresponsive and pulseless; control severe bleeding immediately.
The major life threats identified in the material are airway obstruction, respiratory failure, respiratory arrest, shock, severe bleeding, and cardiac arrest.
Use ABC or CAB according to the presentation rather than mechanically following one order. Several threats may require coordinated actions by the crew.
Determine transport priority during the primary assessment. A detailed history or secondary examination must not delay treatment or transport for an unstable patient.
Recheck the patient after treatment and throughout the call. New threats or failed interventions require immediate correction.

sources.locator: Primary Assessment · Identifying and treating life threats

objectives.objective: List the steps EMTs should follow during the primary assessment of a trauma patient, including examples of abnormal signs and appropriate related actions.
objectives.summary: A trauma primary assessment prioritizes hemorrhage, airway, breathing, circulation, and a rapid scan for additional life threats.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Trauma sequence
bullets: Use the mechanism and findings to consider spinal injury and protect the spine while assessing the patient.
Form a general impression, determine responsiveness, and scan for uncontrolled external bleeding. Apply immediate bleeding control.
Assess and open the airway. Use jaw-thrust when spinal injury is suspected, but maintain an effective airway even if another maneuver becomes necessary.
Assess respiratory rate, depth, effort, and chest movement. Provide oxygen or assisted ventilation according to oxygenation and ventilation findings.
Assess pulse, skin, and perfusion. Treat life threats as you find them rather than waiting until the examination ends.
Perform a rapid 60–90-second scan to identify injuries that need management or protection before transport. This is not the detailed secondary examination.
Establish transport priority and continue assessment during transport when appropriate. Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, bleeding control, and other interventions.

objectives.objective: Explain the process for determining the priority of patient care and transport at an emergency scene and include examples of conditions that necessitate immediate transport.
objectives.summary: Transport priority is determined during the primary assessment. Immediate transport matters when the patient needs definitive treatment you cannot provide on scene.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Transport priority
bullets: High-priority findings include unresponsiveness, altered level of consciousness, difficulty breathing, and uncontrolled bleeding.
Severe chest pain, pale skin or other signs of poor perfusion, complicated childbirth, and severe pain elsewhere are also listed as high-priority findings.
Treat immediate life threats first and coordinate transport while care continues. Do not let a lengthy history or detailed physical exam delay an unstable patient.
Transport decisions depend on condition, available advanced care, transport distance, and local protocols.
The Golden Hour or Golden Period describes the time from injury to definitive care, when timely treatment of shock and traumatic injuries is crucial.
A patient who appears stable can still be potentially unstable. Continue evaluating because worsening mental status, breathing, circulation, or bleeding changes priority.
When time is limited, the secondary examination may occur en route or may yield to continued management of life threats.

objectives.objective: Discuss the importance of protecting a trauma patient’s spine and identifying fractured extremities during patient packaging for transport.
objectives.summary: Protect a suspected spinal injury during assessment and movement, and assess extremity injuries for nerve or circulation problems before transport.

sections.heading: Primary Assessment · Packaging and spinal protection
bullets: Consider spinal injury from the mechanism, head or neck trauma, pain, neurologic complaints, or an unreliable examination in an altered patient.
Maintain spinal precautions during assessment and coordinated movement. When the posterior body must be examined, use team assistance for a controlled log roll.
Airway patency remains essential. Use jaw-thrust when spinal injury is suspected, but do not leave the airway obstructed if the maneuver fails.
Inspect limbs for symmetry, deformity, swelling, cuts, bruises, and bleeding. Palpate gently for tenderness or abnormalities.
Assess distal pulses, sensation, and motor function. Compare sides to detect weakness, numbness, or unequal circulation.
Findings guide protection of injuries and packaging. Recheck interventions and patient condition after movement.
Packaging must support prompt transport when life threats are present; it should not substitute for continued assessment of airway, breathing, circulation, or hemorrhage.

objectives.objective: Discuss the process of taking a focused history, its key components, and its relationship to the primary assessment process.
objectives.summary: A focused history explains the current complaint and relevant background after immediate life threats have been addressed.

sections.heading: History Taking · Focused history
bullets: Start with introductions, respectful communication, and permission to treat. Ask an open-ended question to identify why the patient called today.

OPQRST: Onset—when and how it began; Provocation/palliation—what worsens or relieves it; Quality—what it feels like; Region/radiation—where it is and spreads; Severity—0–10 rating; Timing—duration and changes.

SAMPLE: Signs/symptoms—current observed and reported problems; Allergies—known reactions; Medications—prescription, over-the-counter, supplements, and relevant drug use; Pertinent history—illnesses or surgery; Last oral intake—food/drink; Events—what happened before symptoms or injury.
Record important context, including incident date, age, current health status, and relevant past history.
Document pertinent negatives: relevant symptoms or findings that are absent. Their absence can help interpret the complaint even though no intervention is needed for the absent finding.
Use relatives, witnesses, medical alert jewelry, medication lists, and other scene clues when the patient cannot answer.
The history expands on the primary assessment; it does not take priority over treatment of an obstructed airway, inadequate breathing, severe bleeding, or another immediate threat.

sources.locator: History of present illness and collateral sources

objectives.objective: Describe examples of different techniques EMTs may use to obtain information from patients during the history-taking process.
objectives.summary: Use respectful, simple questions and adapt communication to the patient’s abilities. Confirm understanding and seek reliable additional sources when needed.

sections.heading: History Taking · Communication techniques
bullets: Begin with an open-ended question and allow the patient to describe the complaint. Use eye contact and repeat the explanation back in your own words to confirm it.
Use short, direct, closed-ended questions when the patient is silent, overwhelmed, or unable to give a long answer. Gently redirect an overly talkative patient.
Keep questions simple for cognitive limitations; avoid medical jargon and use caregivers for information about baseline function.
Seek an interpreter for a language barrier. If one is unavailable, determine whether the patient understands your role and use brief questions and gestures.
For hearing difficulty, speak slowly and clearly or use writing. For visual impairment, identify yourself verbally, explain each step, and warn before moving the patient.
If the patient cannot answer, ask relatives or witnesses and inspect medical alert jewelry and written history or medication lists.
Prioritize the most serious complaint when several symptoms are reported. Observe nonverbal behavior as well as the words used.

objectives.objective: Discuss different challenges EMTs may face when taking a patient history on sensitive topics and strategies they may use to facilitate each situation.
objectives.summary: Sensitive history requires privacy, calm communication, and a nonjudgmental approach. Behavior may reflect a medical emergency rather than a personality problem.

sections.heading: History Taking · Sensitive topics and challenges
bullets: Alcohol or drugs: answers may be incomplete or unreliable. Ask professionally without arguing or judging; consider medical causes of confusion and collect additional clues.
Abuse or violence: document observations and statements accurately, follow reporting laws and local protocols, and involve the appropriate authorities without making accusations.

Reproductive or urinary concerns: explain why questions are needed, ask about last menstrual period or urinary symptoms when relevant, and consider pregnancy in a childbearing-age patient with lower abdominal pain.
Anxiety can accompany hypoglycemia, shock, or hypoxia. Assess the medical problem before assuming it is purely emotional.
Crying or depression: remain patient, reassuring, and a good listener. Anger or intoxication: avoid confrontation and retreat if safety is threatened.
Confusing history: consider hypoxia, stroke, diabetes, trauma, medications, or drug effects. Seek information about the normal baseline.
Adapt for cultural preferences, language, hearing, vision, or cognitive limitations without compromising urgent care.

objectives.objective: Describe the purpose of a secondary assessment and a physical exam; include how to determine which aspects of the physical exam to use, and the steps.
objectives.summary: The secondary assessment searches systematically for additional injuries or causes after immediate life threats have been addressed. Choose its scope from the patient’s condition and complaint.

sections.heading: Secondary Assessment · Purpose and examination
bullets: A stable patient with an isolated complaint may receive a focused examination at the scene. Other patients may need a broader systematic examination.
If the patient needs urgent transport, examine en route when possible. Continued management of life threats may leave no time for a full secondary assessment.
Inspection means looking for abnormalities; palpation means feeling for them; auscultation means listening with a stethoscope.
Use DCAP-BTLS for injury findings: Deformities, Contusions, Abrasions, Punctures or penetrations, Burns, Tenderness, Lacerations, and Swelling.
Compare sides when appropriate and examine the head and neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, and posterior body according to the required scope.
Assess vital signs and use monitoring devices to add information. Devices supplement the clinical examination rather than replacing it.
The detailed examination can identify injuries or causes missed in the rapid 60–90-second primary scan. Treat newly found threats promptly.

sources.locator: Secondary Assessment · Examination methods and DCAP-BTLS

objectives.objective: Explain situations in which patients may receive a focused assessment, including examples by body system of what each focused assessment should include based on a patient’s chief complaint.
objectives.summary: A focused assessment targets the body region or system affected by the chief complaint, usually in a responsive medical patient or a patient with a nonsignificant injury mechanism.

sections.heading: Secondary Assessment · Focused systems
bullets: Respiratory: expose the chest appropriately, check airway and neck or chest trauma, compare chest symmetry, listen to bilateral breath sounds, and assess rate, rhythm, depth, effort, retractions, and accessory muscles.
Cardiovascular: assess pulse rate, rhythm, and quality; respiratory rate; blood pressure; skin findings; and distal pulses on both sides. Look for chest injury and consider the breath sounds.

Neurologic: assess responsiveness, orientation, GCS when appropriate, speech, movement, pupil size and light response, and bilateral strength and sensation. Indications include altered status, head injury, dizziness, drowsiness, stupor, or syncope.
Abdominal: assess the four quadrants for tenderness, rigidity, and guarding with gentle palpation.
Extremity or musculoskeletal: inspect for deformity, swelling, wounds, and bleeding; assess tenderness, distal pulse, sensation, and movement.
Use monitoring information such as SpO2, glucose, or blood pressure as relevant. A focused examination must not prevent a broader assessment if the history or findings suggest additional problems.

objectives.objective: List normal blood pressure ranges for adults, children, and infants.
objectives.summary: Use age-specific systolic ranges. The supplied normal-pressure table gives systolic values rather than paired systolic/diastolic ranges.

sections.heading: Secondary Assessment · Normal blood pressure
bullets: Adult: 90–120 mm Hg systolic.
Adolescent, age 15 years: 110–131 mm Hg systolic.
Child, age 7 years: 97–115 mm Hg systolic.
Child, age 2 years: 86–106 mm Hg systolic.
Infant, age 1–12 months: 72–104 mm Hg systolic.
Neonate, age 96 hours: 67–84 mm Hg systolic.
Hypotension means lower-than-normal blood pressure; hypertension means higher-than-normal pressure.
Interpret the reading with age, baseline, pulse, skin, mental status, and serial trends. A normal pressure alone does not exclude poor perfusion; decreased blood pressure is a late shock sign.
Auscultation can provide systolic and diastolic readings. Palpation identifies systolic pressure only when listening is difficult.

objectives.objective: Explain the importance of performing a reassessment of the patient and the steps in this process.
objectives.summary: Reassessment detects improvement, deterioration, and failed interventions. Repeat it throughout care, especially after treatment or movement.

sections.heading: Reassessment · Steps and timing
bullets: Repeat the primary assessment, including mental status, airway, breathing, circulation, and bleeding control.
Repeat vital signs and compare them with baseline and earlier readings. Look for trends instead of interpreting each value in isolation.
Revisit the chief complaint: has the symptom improved, worsened, or changed? Ask about new problems.
Recheck every intervention. Confirm that airway support, oxygen or ventilation, hemorrhage control, and other treatment are still effective.
Identify and treat changes promptly, and document the findings and response.
The outline and detailed reassessment lecture specify approximately every 5 minutes for unstable patients and every 15 minutes for stable patients.
Reassess sooner when the patient deteriorates or an intervention may have failed; scheduled intervals are not a reason to wait.

sources.locator: Detailed reassessment timing and concluding example

objectives.gap: The concluding spoken example says 5 or 10 minutes, while the outline and the same lecture’s detailed teaching say 5 minutes unstable and 15 minutes stable. The answer uses the repeated detailed timing; confirm the concluding example with the instructor.

sections.heading: Clarifying reassessment timing
paragraphs: The NHTSA curriculum corroborates the detailed class teaching: reassess and record stable patients at least every 15 minutes and unstable patients at least every 5 minutes. Recheck after interventions and sooner when the condition changes; do not wait for the interval when deterioration is evident.

outside.note: The outside source supports 5/15 but cannot resolve what the instructor meant by the spoken 5-or-10-minute example.

objectives.objective: Describe the major structures of the respiratory system.
objectives.summary: The upper airway conditions incoming air; the lower airway carries it to alveoli, where gases exchange with pulmonary blood.

sections.heading: Anatomy of the Respiratory System
bullets: Upper airway: nose, mouth, oral cavity, pharynx, and laryngeal structures. Its main functions are warming, filtering, and humidifying incoming air.
The pharynx has nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx regions. The epiglottis helps keep swallowed material from entering the larynx.
The larynx includes thyroid cartilage, cricoid cartilage, the cricothyroid membrane, vocal cords, and the glottic opening. The vocal-cord level marks the upper/lower airway boundary.
The trachea runs from below the cricoid into the chest and divides at the carina into right and left main bronchi.
Bronchi branch into smaller bronchi and bronchioles. Smooth muscle in bronchioles allows narrowing or dilation.
Alveoli are thin-walled sacs surrounded by pulmonary capillaries. Oxygen diffuses into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli for exhalation.
The diaphragm is a principal breathing muscle; the phrenic nerve enables its contraction. Chest movement supports lung expansion.

objectives.objective: Discuss the physiology of breathing.
objectives.summary: Ventilation moves air, oxygenation loads oxygen onto hemoglobin, and respiration exchanges gases. Effective oxygen delivery also requires circulation.

sections.heading: Physiology of Breathing
bullets: Inhalation is active: the diaphragm and intercostals contract, thoracic volume increases, and pressure falls so air moves into the lungs.
Quiet exhalation is normally passive: breathing muscles relax, thoracic volume decreases, and pressure rises above outside pressure so air moves out.
Tidal volume is air moved in one breath, about 500 mL for an average adult. Dead-space air does not reach alveoli for gas exchange.
Oxygenation loads oxygen onto hemoglobin. Ventilating in oxygen-depleted air may not produce adequate oxygenation.
External respiration exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide between alveoli and pulmonary capillaries. Internal respiration exchanges gases between systemic blood and tissue cells.
Surfactant helps keep alveoli expanded. Ventilation and perfusion must reach the same area for effective exchange.
Chemoreceptor feedback, including carbon dioxide and hydrogen-ion levels, influences brain respiratory centers. Inadequate oxygen leads to hypoxia and less effective anaerobic metabolism.

objectives.objective: Give the signs of adequate breathing.
objectives.summary: Adequate breathing requires an appropriate rate, sufficient depth, regular pattern, and effective air movement. Rate alone is not enough.

sections.heading: Patient Assessment · Adequate breathing
bullets: For adults, the supplied normal breathing range is 12–20 breaths/min.
Inhalation and exhalation should have a regular pattern without abnormal pauses or gasping.
Chest rise and fall should be regular and equal on both sides. Adequate tidal volume produces visible, appropriate chest movement.
Breath sounds should be clear and equal bilaterally.
Assess depth and effort as well as rate. A normal count with very shallow breaths can still produce inadequate ventilation.
Check mental status, skin color, and oxygen saturation to assess oxygenation. Apparently adequate air movement does not guarantee adequate gas exchange or tissue oxygen delivery.
Continue observing the patient. A pattern that was adequate initially may deteriorate with fatigue, worsening obstruction, or illness.
A patient who moves air adequately but remains hypoxic may need supplemental oxygen; a patient with inadequate air movement needs ventilation support.

objectives.objective: Give the signs of inadequate breathing.
objectives.summary: Inadequate breathing is identified from air movement and the whole presentation. Abnormal rate, shallow depth, fatigue, or altered mental status can signal urgent need for support.

sections.heading: Patient Assessment · Abnormal breathing
bullets: Abnormal adult findings include fewer than 12 breaths/min or more than 20/min with shortness of breath, an irregular rhythm, and diminished, absent, or noisy breath sounds.
Look for reduced airflow at the nose or mouth, unequal or insufficient chest expansion, shallow breaths, and reduced tidal volume.
Accessory-muscle use and retractions show increased effort. Pale, cyanotic, cool, or moist skin may accompany inadequate breathing.
Altered mental status, inadequate minute volume, and respiratory fatigue are signs that support may be needed.
Agonal gasps are ineffective occasional gasps and can occur after cardiac arrest. Do not mistake them for normal breathing.
Cheyne–Stokes breathing increases in rate and depth then includes apnea; ataxic breathing is irregular; Kussmaul breathing is deep and rapid in metabolic acidosis.
Open and clear the airway, supply needed oxygen, and provide ventilatory support when air movement is inadequate.

objectives.objective: Describe the assessment and care of a patient with apnea.
objectives.summary: Apnea means absent breathing. Open the airway, assess circulation, and begin artificial ventilation immediately when the patient has a pulse but is not breathing.

sections.heading: Patient Assessment · Apnea and artificial ventilation
bullets: Rapidly assess airway patency, breathing, and pulse. Position the patient supine; move as a unit when spinal injury is possible.
Open the airway with head tilt–chin lift when spinal trauma is not suspected, or jaw-thrust when it is. Clear secretions or visible obstruction as necessary.
Begin artificial ventilation with a mouth-to-mask or bag-mask device. Use an appropriate airway adjunct when indicated and supplemental oxygen.
For an apneic patient with a pulse, the airway outline gives adults 1 breath every 6 seconds and children or infants 1 breath every 2–3 seconds.
Deliver a slow, gentle breath over about 1 second, using enough volume for visible chest rise and allowing exhalation.
If the patient is pulseless, begin CPR rather than treating the problem as isolated apnea.
Continue reassessment of chest rise, airway patency, pulse, oxygenation, and effectiveness. Excessively rapid or forceful breaths increase complications.

sources.locator: VI. Opening the Airway; XII. Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Apneic ventilation rates

objectives.objective: Explain how to assess for adequate and inadequate respiration, including the use of pulse oximetry.
objectives.summary: Assess ventilation and oxygenation separately. Pulse oximetry estimates hemoglobin oxygen saturation but cannot prove adequate ventilation or cellular respiration.

sections.heading: Patient Assessment · Respiration and monitoring
bullets: Observe rate, rhythm, depth, equal chest movement, breath sounds, effort, mental status, and skin color. Consider environmental causes such as altitude, carbon monoxide, or an enclosed space.
SpO2 is the estimated percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen. The supplied airway material gives normal room-air saturation greater than 94%.
Readings may lag for up to 60 seconds. Do not delay support when the clinical examination shows respiratory insufficiency.
Hypovolemia, vasoconstriction, hypothermia, dirty fingers, dark or metallic polish, and carbon monoxide can make readings inaccurate.
Pulse oximetry does not measure ventilation effectiveness or cellular metabolism. A normal-looking number does not replace the examination.
End-tidal CO2 is the concentration at the end of exhalation. Capnometry gives a number; capnography adds a waveform. The supplied normal range is 35–45 mm Hg.
Interpret CO2 with ventilation, perfusion, and metabolism; a low value can reflect hyperventilation or reduced CO2 delivery to the lungs.

objectives.objective: Explain how to assess for a patent airway.
objectives.summary: A patent airway permits air passage. Assess it directly and repeatedly; breathing sounds and responsiveness help identify obstruction.

sections.heading: Opening the Airway · Patency assessment
bullets: In an unconscious patient, rapidly assess airway patency, breathing adequacy, and pulse. Position supine as needed while protecting a possible spinal injury.
The tongue is the most common obstruction in an unconscious patient because relaxed muscles allow it to fall back into the throat.
Look in the mouth for visible blood, vomit, mucus, loose dental material, food, or another obstruction.
Gurgling suggests fluid needing suction. Snoring and other abnormal upper-airway sounds require assessment and airway correction.
Open the airway with the appropriate maneuver. Clear fluid with suction and remove only visible material; avoid blind finger sweeps.
Reassess airflow and chest movement after opening or clearing the airway. A technically completed maneuver is not proof that it worked.
Continue checking during treatment and transport. Position changes, secretions, swelling, or reduced responsiveness can obstruct a previously open airway.

sources.locator: VI. Opening the Airway; VII. Suctioning; XV. Airway Obstruction

objectives.objective: Describe how to perform the head tilt–chin lift maneuver.
objectives.summary: Head tilt–chin lift opens the airway by moving the jaw and tongue away from the throat. It is the usual maneuver when spinal trauma is not suspected.

sections.heading: Opening the Airway · Head tilt–chin lift
bullets: Position the patient supine and place yourself beside the head.
Place the heel of one hand on the forehead and apply firm backward pressure with the palm.
Place the fingertips of the other hand beneath the lower jaw.
Lift the chin and lower jaw upward while tilting the head back.
Reassess patency and air movement, and inspect for material that needs suctioning or removal. Opening the airway does not remove fluids or foreign material.
When spinal trauma is suspected, use jaw-thrust initially to limit neck movement. The patient assessment material permits head tilt–chin lift if jaw-thrust does not open the airway.
Maintain the open position while providing needed ventilation or adjunct support. The airway can close again if support is released in an unresponsive patient.

sources.locator: VI. Opening the Airway · Head tilt–chin lift

objectives.objective: Describe how to perform the jaw-thrust maneuver.
objectives.summary: Jaw-thrust moves the lower jaw forward to open the airway while limiting head and neck movement when cervical injury is suspected.

sections.heading: Opening the Airway · Jaw-thrust
bullets: Position yourself above the patient’s head.
Place your fingers behind the angles of the lower jaw.
Move the jaw upward and forward. Use the thumbs to help position the lower jaw and open the mouth as needed.
Maintain protection of the cervical spine during the maneuver and coordinated patient movement.
Check whether the airway has actually opened by assessing airflow, breathing, and chest movement. Suction or clear visible material when necessary.
If jaw-thrust cannot establish a patent airway, the patient assessment material directs using head tilt–chin lift. Do not allow a persistent airway obstruction solely to avoid all neck movement.
Jaw-thrust addresses tongue-related obstruction, but it does not correct blood, vomit, swelling, or a foreign object. Continue assessment and use the appropriate additional treatment.

objectives.objective: Explain the importance and techniques of suctioning.
objectives.summary: Suction removes fluid and secretions so ventilation does not push them into the lungs. Limit each attempt and reoxygenate between attempts.

sections.heading: Suctioning · Equipment and technique
bullets: Gurgling is a clue that suction is needed. Use PPE appropriate for airway secretions and aerosol exposure.
Inspect and assemble the device, test suction, and attach the appropriate catheter. A fixed unit should provide over 40 L/min airflow and over 300 mm Hg vacuum with the tubing clamped.
Rigid tonsil/Yankauer tips are suited to the mouth; soft French or whistle-tip catheters are useful for the nose or when a rigid tip cannot be used.
Measure before insertion, using the OPA sizing method described as corner of mouth to earlobe or angle of jaw. Avoid touching the back of the airway and triggering gagging.
Maximum attempt times: adult 15 seconds, child 10 seconds, infant 5 seconds. Reoxygenate and ventilate before repeating; rinse tubing to prevent clogging.
If material cannot be suctioned, remove the catheter, log roll the patient, and carefully remove visible material with a gloved finger.
For rapidly recurring frothy secretions, alternate age-limited suction with about 2 minutes of ventilation.

sources.locator: Suction sizing, time limits, solid material, and recurring froth

objectives.objective: Explain how to measure and insert an oropharyngeal (oral) airway.
objectives.summary: An OPA holds the tongue away from the airway in an unresponsive patient without a gag reflex. Correct size and tolerance are essential.

sections.heading: Basic Airway Adjuncts · OPA
bullets: Use for an unresponsive patient without a gag reflex, whether breathing or apneic, including during bag-mask ventilation.
Do not use in a conscious patient or anyone with an intact gag reflex, because it can trigger gagging and vomiting.
Select length using the corner of the mouth to the earlobe or angle of the jaw, as described in the airway lecture’s sizing discussion.
An airway that is too large may push the tongue backward. One that is too small may act as an obstruction itself.

The lecture describes inserting with the curve upward and rotating 180 degrees as it advances. It also describes an alternative sideways insertion with 90-degree rotation when the usual method is difficult.

Reassess airway patency and ventilation after placement. The device helps maintain a passage and facilitates suctioning; it does not replace airway positioning, secretion clearance, or ventilation support.

sources.locator: VIII. Basic Airway Adjuncts · Oropharyngeal airways
OPA size measurement referenced during suction; indications and rotational insertion

objectives.objective: Describe how to measure and insert a nasopharyngeal (nasal) airway.
objectives.summary: An NPA may be tolerated when the patient has a gag reflex and cannot maintain the airway. Lubricate it and insert gently; stop if resistance or bleeding occurs.

sections.heading: Basic Airway Adjuncts · NPA
bullets: An NPA is a soft tube introduced through a nostril to help maintain an airway passage.
Indications include semiconscious or unconscious patients with an intact gag reflex and patients who will not tolerate an OPA.
Avoid it with severe head injury and blood draining from the nose or a history of nasal fracture. The lecture also flags possible skull injury with clear fluid from the nose.
The lecture says to lubricate before insertion and insert gently, usually through the right nostril unless resistance prevents this.
If resistance or bleeding occurs, stop and reassess rather than forcing the tube.
Continue assessing airflow and the patient’s response. An NPA supports patency but does not provide ventilation or remove secretions.
The supplied material refers to a skill drill but does not state the complete sizing landmarks or a full insertion sequence.

sources.locator: VIII. Basic Airway Adjuncts · Nasopharyngeal airways
NPA indications, lubrication, precautions and gentle insertion

objectives.gap: The supplied files do not enumerate NPA measurement landmarks or the full insertion sequence. Those procedural details require the class skill material.

sections.heading: NPA sizing and insertion
bullets: Check indication and contraindications first. Suspected basilar skull fracture is a contraindication; significant nasal trauma also requires caution and protocol guidance.
Estimate length from the tip of the nose to the tragus of the ear; reassess ventilation after placement. Use the sizing method taught for the specific device in skills lab.
Inspect both nostrils and select the wider passage. Clear obstructing secretions as needed and lubricate the airway with water-soluble lubricant.
Insert gently backward along the floor of the nose, not upward. Keep the bevel facing the nasal septum.
Advance until the flange rests against the nostril. If resistance persists, stop and try the other nostril; never force insertion.
Reassess airway sounds and ventilation. An NPA helps maintain patency but does not replace effective assisted ventilation when breathing is inadequate.

objectives.objective: Explain the use of the recovery position to maintain a clear airway.
objectives.summary: The recovery position helps keep the airway clear in an unconscious, uninjured patient who is breathing adequately without assistance.

sections.heading: Maintaining the Airway · Recovery position
bullets: Use it when the patient is unconscious, has no injury, and is breathing spontaneously at a normal rate with adequate tidal volume.
The lecture describes rolling the patient onto the side. This helps keep the relaxed tongue from obstructing the airway.
The side position also allows saliva or vomit to drain from the mouth rather than collect and be aspirated.
Confirm adequate spontaneous breathing before choosing this approach. The position does not replace artificial ventilation when air movement is inadequate.
Do not apply the uninjured-patient approach without considering possible trauma or spinal injury.
Continue observing airway patency, breathing rate and depth, secretions, and mental status. If breathing worsens, reassess and provide the needed airway or ventilation support.
Suction may still be required. The recovery position assists drainage but is not proof that all fluid or obstruction has cleared.

sources.locator: Recovery position, tongue obstruction, and drainage

objectives.objective: Describe the importance of giving supplemental oxygen to patients who are hypoxic.
objectives.summary: Hypoxia means tissues are not receiving enough oxygen. Provide needed supplemental oxygen, and add ventilation support when breathing itself is inadequate.

sections.heading: Supplemental Oxygen · Hypoxia
bullets: The brain, heart, lungs, kidneys, and liver require a continuous oxygen supply. Inadequate delivery can rapidly impair their function.
Do not withhold oxygen from a patient who needs it, especially while assisting ventilation. A concern about hypoxic drive is not a reason to leave a hypoxic patient untreated.
Distinguish oxygenation from ventilation: oxygen increases available oxygen; bag-mask support moves air when breathing is absent or inadequate.
Use pulse oximetry together with the clinical examination to tailor treatment. The supplied material recommends the minimum oxygen needed to maintain saturation at or above 94%.
Not every patient requires high-flow oxygen. Excessive oxygen can be harmful in some illnesses, but hypoxemia is the greater immediate danger when oxygen is needed.
For suspected myocardial infarction, the material identifies oxygen when there is shortness of breath, heart-failure signs, or room-air SpO2 below 94%. Shock also warrants oxygen.
Reassess the response and adjust support when oxygenation or ventilation deteriorates.

objectives.objective: Discuss the basics of how oxygen is stored and the various hazards associated with its use.
objectives.summary: Medical oxygen is commonly stored as compressed gas. Secure cylinders and keep ignition sources away because oxygen accelerates combustion.

sections.heading: Supplemental Oxygen · Storage and safety
bullets: Common portable supplies are D or jumbo D green steel or aluminum cylinders. Verify the medical-oxygen label rather than relying on color alone.
Check test markings. The material gives aluminum cylinders a 5-year test interval and composite cylinders a 3-year interval.
Cylinder duration depends on remaining pressure and the selected flow rate. Liquid oxygen is another storage method.
Secure stored and in-use cylinders. A damaged pressurized cylinder can become a projectile; never leave one standing unattended.
The pin-index system helps prevent a portable regulator being connected to the wrong gas. Larger cylinders use gas-specific threaded connections.
A regulator reduces pressure, usually to 40–70 psi; a flowmeter sets liters per minute. A pressure-compensated float flowmeter must stay upright; a Bourdon gauge can work in any position.
Oxygen does not itself burn, but speeds combustion. Keep flames and sparks away and ventilate the area.
Avoid unnecessary excessive oxygen and reassess clinical need and saturation.

objectives.objective: Explain the use of a nonrebreathing mask and the oxygen flow requirements for its use.
objectives.summary: A nonrebreathing mask supplies high-concentration oxygen to a significantly hypoxemic patient who is breathing adequately. It does not ventilate an apneic patient.

sections.heading: Oxygen-Delivery Equipment · Nonrebreathing mask
bullets: The mask uses a reservoir bag and one-way valve arrangement to make oxygen available during inhalation.
Exhaled gas exits through ports at the cheeks; valves limit rebreathing of exhaled gas.
Fill the reservoir before placing the mask on the patient.
Use enough flow to keep the bag from collapsing during inspiration, usually 10–15 L/min. If it collapses, increase flow.
Select an appropriate adult, pediatric, or infant size and monitor fit, comfort, respiratory effort, and oxygenation.
Remove the mask when oxygen therapy is discontinued rather than leaving it on without flow.
If air movement becomes inadequate, provide ventilation support. A high oxygen concentration cannot substitute for the movement of air into and out of the lungs.
Continue reassessing both the patient and the supply, especially during movement or prolonged transport.

objectives.objective: Describe the indications for using a nasal cannula rather than a nonrebreathing face mask.
objectives.summary: A nasal cannula is a lower-concentration option for mild hypoxemia or a patient who cannot tolerate a mask, provided breathing is adequate.

sections.heading: Oxygen-Delivery Equipment · Nasal cannula
bullets: Two prongs deliver oxygen through the nostrils. The material gives 1–6 L/min, producing approximately 24–44% inspired oxygen.
Conventional flow above 6 L/min is not recommended for comfort.
Use it for mild hypoxemia rather than the significantly hypoxemic patient who needs the higher concentration available from a nonrebreathing mask.
The patient must still be breathing adequately. Inadequate ventilation requires assisted breathing, not simply changing between oxygen-delivery devices.
The lecture also describes it as useful when a face mask is not tolerated.
Nasal obstruction or breathing through the mouth can reduce the oxygen delivered by this method in the course description.
Check placement and reassess saturation, work of breathing, chest movement, and mental status. Escalate support if oxygenation or breathing worsens.
Humidification may be considered by some systems for extended transport, with attention to aerosol exposure.

objectives.objective: Describe the indications for use of a humidifier during supplemental oxygen therapy.
objectives.summary: Humidification adds moisture to supplemental oxygen and may be used during extended transport, but it can increase aerosol exposure.

sections.heading: Oxygen-Delivery Equipment · Humidification
bullets: Some EMS systems supply humidified oxygen for patients receiving oxygen over an extended transport.
The airway’s normal conditioning function includes humidifying incoming air. Supplemental oxygen equipment may include a humidifier to add moisture.
The supplied material associates humidification with increased production of aerosolized fluid droplets capable of transmitting disease.
Balance comfort and the system’s practice with exposure precautions. Use appropriate PPE for the airway task being performed.
Humidification does not change the need to select an appropriate oxygen device and flow or to assess ventilation adequacy.
Continue checking oxygen delivery, patient tolerance, saturation, and work of breathing. If the patient needs assisted ventilation, adding moisture is not a substitute for that support.
The material gives extended transport as the use case; it does not establish a specific transport-duration cutoff.

sources.locator: XI. Oxygen-Delivery Equipment · Nasal cannulas and extended-transport humidification

objectives.objective: Describe how to perform mouth-to-mouth or mouth-to-mask ventilation.
objectives.summary: Mouth-to-mask ventilation provides artificial breaths through a barrier mask, with an oxygen inlet when available. Effective breaths require an open airway and visible chest rise.

sections.heading: Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Mouth-to-mask
bullets: Once absent breathing is identified, begin artificial ventilation promptly after opening and clearing the airway.
A barrier device is routinely used for mouth-to-mouth ventilation. A mask with an oxygen inlet can supply oxygen during mouth-to-mask ventilation.
Give slow, gentle breaths over approximately 1 second using enough volume to see chest rise, and allow the patient to exhale.
For an apneic patient with a pulse, the supplied rates are adult 1 breath every 6 seconds; child or infant 1 every 2–3 seconds.
Avoid forceful or rapid delivery. Poor airway position and excessive rate or volume can push air into the stomach and cause vomiting or aspiration.
Reassess the airway and effectiveness if the chest does not rise or resistance is felt.
The supplied files describe the barrier and breath-delivery principles but do not enumerate a complete mouth-to-mouth procedural sequence.

sources.locator: XII. Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Mouth-to-mouth/mask and gastric distention

objectives.gap: The complete mouth-to-mouth sequence is not provided in the uploaded files. The answer covers the supplied barrier, oxygen-inlet, rate, volume, and reassessment principles.

sections.heading: Adult mouth-to-mouth and mouth-to-mask steps
bullets: Open the airway. For mouth-to-mouth, pinch the nose and make an airtight seal over the mouth. For a pocket mask, seal it over the nose and mouth while maintaining the open airway.
Give each breath over about 1 second, using enough air for visible chest rise. Take a normal breath yourself; avoid large or rapid breaths.
During adult CPR without an advanced airway, use 30 compressions followed by 2 breaths. For an adult with a pulse but respiratory arrest, give 1 breath every 6 seconds.

sources.title: American Heart Association — 2025 Adult Basic Life Support

objectives.objective: Describe the use of a one- or two-person bag-mask device.
objectives.summary: Bag-mask ventilation requires a patent airway, a good seal, and controlled breaths producing chest rise. Correct the seal and position before forcing additional volume.

sections.heading: Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Bag-mask device
bullets: Connect oxygen at 15 L/min with the reservoir and a properly fitted mask to provide high-concentration oxygen.
For one-person technique, the lecture describes an E-C clamp: thumb and index finger hold the mask while the other fingers lift the jaw; the other hand squeezes the bag.
Give gentle breaths over about 1 second, with enough volume for chest rise and time for exhalation. For apnea with a pulse, use the supplied adult 6-second interval or pediatric 2–3-second interval.

When assisting spontaneous inadequate breathing, explain the procedure and initially synchronize squeezing with the patient’s breaths. After 5–10 breaths, adjust rate and volume toward adequate minute ventilation.
Watch chest movement and reassess airway patency, mask seal, breath sounds, and oxygenation.
Excessive pressure, rate, or volume can reduce venous return and cause gastric distention.
The source material references the bag-mask skill drill but does not enumerate the full two-person procedure.

sources.locator: XII. Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Bag-mask and synchronized assistance

objectives.gap: The uploaded material does not enumerate the complete two-person bag-mask sequence.

sections.heading: Adult bag-mask teamwork
bullets: With two rescuers, one uses both hands to open the airway and seal the mask; the second squeezes the bag. Both watch for chest rise and fall.
With one rescuer, use one hand to maintain the mask seal and lift the jaw while the other squeezes the bag. The two-rescuer technique is more effective when help is available.
Use visible chest rise to judge each breath and avoid excessive rate or volume. Correct the seal and airway position if ventilation is ineffective.

sources.title: American Heart Association — 2025 Adult Basic Life Support

objectives.objective: Describe the signs associated with adequate and inadequate artificial ventilation.
objectives.summary: Effective artificial ventilation produces chest rise and adequate air movement without excessive pressure. Ongoing observation is needed to detect obstruction, leakage, and complications.

sections.heading: Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Effectiveness and complications
bullets: Observe chest rise and fall with each breath and assess the patient’s oxygenation and overall response. Deliver only the volume needed for appropriate visible rise.
Little chest movement, unequal expansion, resistance, persistent hypoxia, or worsening mental status suggests ineffective support and requires reassessment.
Check airway position and patency, suction when needed, and correct the mask seal. Do not respond to poor chest rise simply by squeezing harder.
Use slow, gentle breaths over about 1 second at the appropriate rate. Allow exhalation before the next breath.
Positive pressure raises intrathoracic pressure and can reduce blood return to the heart and cardiac output. Excessive ventilation increases this risk.
Forceful or rapid breaths and an obstructed or poorly positioned airway can cause gastric distention, vomiting, and aspiration.
If vomiting occurs, turn the body to the side, clear or suction the mouth, return supine, and resume needed ventilation with appropriate spinal protection.

sources.locator: Assisted and Artificial Ventilation · Effectiveness and complications

objectives.objective: Describe the use of continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).
objectives.summary: CPAP supports an alert, spontaneously breathing patient in respiratory distress by maintaining airway pressure, particularly during exhalation. It is not a replacement for ventilation in apnea.

sections.heading: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure
bullets: Pressure helps open collapsed alveoli, improves gas exchange, and can move interstitial fluid back toward the pulmonary circulation. The mask needs a good seal.

Candidates must be alert and able to follow commands. The material lists moderate-to-severe distress from pulmonary edema or COPD, distress after submersion, rapid breathing impairing minute volume, and SpO2 below 90%.
Do not use for apnea, agonal gasps, hypoventilation, inability to protect the airway or follow commands, hypotension, or inability to speak.

Other listed exclusions include pneumothorax/chest trauma, facial trauma, active vomiting or gastrointestinal bleeding, cardiogenic shock, tracheostomy, inability to sit upright, poor mask fit, or mask intolerance.
Use a full oxygen cylinder when oxygen drives the unit. The supplied typical pressure range is 7–10 cm H2O.
Monitor blood pressure, breathing, and mental status. Positive pressure can lower cardiac output; pneumothorax is another potential complication.
Coach rather than force an anxious patient. If deterioration occurs, remove CPAP and provide bag-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen.

objectives.objective: Explain how to recognize and care for a foreign body airway obstruction.
objectives.summary: Differentiate effective coughing from poor air exchange or severe obstruction. Support effective coughing, but act promptly when the patient cannot move enough air.

sections.heading: Airway Obstruction · Recognition and care
bullets: Mild obstruction with good exchange: the patient can breathe, talk, or cough forcefully. Do not interfere with effective efforts to expel the object; monitor continuously.
Poor exchange: weak cough, increased difficulty breathing, stridor, or cyanosis. Treat as severe obstruction rather than waiting for complete blockage.
Severe obstruction: cannot breathe, talk, or cough, little or no air movement, possible throat-clutching and cyanosis.
For a conscious patient with foreign-body obstruction, the supplied airway outline describes abdominal thrusts until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unconscious.
For unresponsive severe obstruction, the outline describes chest compressions followed by inspection for visible material and attempted breaths. Never perform a blind finger sweep.
Suction secretions and remove visible loose material. Leave well-fitting dentures in place if they improve the mask seal; remove loose appliances.
Swelling from allergy or infection and traumatic tissue injury are other obstruction causes; repeated foreign-body maneuvers do not correct them and rapid appropriate care is needed.

objectives.objective: Describe the four-step process of assisting with advanced life support (ALS) skills.
objectives.summary: The EMT supports ALS airway care through preparation, basic airway management, ventilation, and monitoring. The advanced provider performs the advanced airway intervention.

sections.heading: Assisting with ALS Airway Procedures · EMT role
bullets: Help set up equipment while continuing effective BLS airway maneuvers and ventilation. Preparation must not interrupt needed oxygen delivery.

Provide appropriate PPE, functioning suction with rigid and soft catheters, a laryngoscope and blade, ET tube, introducer or stylet, lubricant, syringe, confirmation devices, and securing equipment as requested.
Have alternative airway equipment ready, including a supraglottic device or other ALS fallback equipment.
Assist with preoxygenation using the proper bag-mask seal, ventilation rate, volume, and exhalation time.
Help monitor saturation, end-tidal CO2, ventilation resistance, and clinical signs of perfusion and ventilation after the procedure.
Watch for displacement or improper position and communicate deteriorating findings promptly.
The supplied outline names a six-step BE MAGIC procedure, but does not enumerate the separate four-step assisting process requested in this objective.

sources.locator: XVI. Assisting with ALS Airway Procedures · EMT support and equipment setup

objectives.gap: The named four-step ALS assistance process is not enumerated in the supplied files. BE MAGIC is a separate six-step process, so it must not be presented as that missing four-step answer.

sections.heading: What can be verified
paragraphs: The National EMS Education Standards define minimum competencies and allow educators to choose local curricula and instructional resources. They do not establish the textbook’s named four-step ALS-assistance sequence. The exact labels and task order therefore still require the instructor’s material or the textbook section; an outside general framework should not be presented as that answer.
