objectives.objective: Explain common causes of foreign body airway obstruction in both children and adults and how to distinguish mild or partial airway obstruction from complete airway obstruction.
objectives.summary: Judge airway obstruction by the effectiveness of air exchange, speech, and coughing—not simply by whether an object might be present.

sections.heading: Common causes
bullets: Adults often choke while eating; children often choke during meals or play.
Obstructing material may include food or other foreign objects, dentures, blood, vomit, or damaged tissue.
Relaxed throat muscles in an unresponsive patient can also obstruct the airway, though this is not itself a lodged foreign object.

sections.heading: Mild/partial obstruction
bullets: The patient can move adequate air and may still speak or cough, despite distress.
Do not interfere with an effective cough; observe for worsening.
Provide oxygen when needed/tolerated and arrange transport as described in the pediatric discussion.

sections.heading: Severe/complete obstruction
bullets: The patient suddenly cannot speak or cough effectively, may grasp the throat, become cyanotic, or make exaggerated breathing efforts.
Stridor may occur with severe obstruction, but complete blockage may leave little air movement.
An unresponsive patient with ineffective airway opening and failed ventilations should raise concern for obstruction.
Deterioration changes the intervention: a previously effective cough does not justify continued observation once air exchange becomes inadequate.

sources.locator: XVI. Foreign Body Airway Obstruction in Adults; XVII. Pediatric obstruction

objectives.objective: Describe the different methods for removing a foreign body airway obstruction in an infant, child, and adult, including the procedure for a patient with an obstruction who becomes unresponsive.
objectives.summary: Choose the obstruction maneuver by age and responsiveness; remove only a visible, reachable object and avoid blind finger sweeps.

sections.heading: Responsive patient with severe obstruction
bullets: Adult or child older than 1 year: the supplied class procedure uses abdominal thrusts. For a child, adjust force to body size and work at the child’s level.
Advanced pregnancy or a patient whose body size prevents abdominal thrusts: the class procedure uses chest thrusts.

Infant: no abdominal thrusts. Support the jaw/head with the infant facedown on your forearm, head below the body; give 5 back slaps between the shoulder blades. Turn faceup while supporting the head and give 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the sternum. Repeat as described.

sections.heading: Becomes unresponsive
bullets: Lower the patient safely, activate help, and begin CPR with compressions without delaying for a pulse check in this witnessed choking-collapse sequence.
After compressions, open the airway and look in the mouth. Remove an object only if it is seen and easily reached.
Attempt ventilation and continue compressions/airway checks until relieved or appropriate providers take over.

sections.heading: Found unresponsive
paragraphs: The outline separately describes an initial breathing/pulse check. If a pulse is present but breathing absent, attempt ventilation, reposition after the first failed breath, and suspect obstruction after persistent failure.
bullets: A patient still breathing, coughing, or speaking effectively should not have those efforts interrupted by obstruction maneuvers.

sources.locator: XVI. Adult obstruction; XVII. Infant and child obstruction
Visible-object removal and blind finger sweep prohibition

objectives.gap: The original class materials describe these procedures but contain an overbroad pediatric instruction about not dislodging an object. Their mild-versus-severe distinction is necessary.

sections.heading: Current choking sequence — AHA/AAP 2025
bullets: Effective cough/speech: encourage coughing and monitor. Weak/absent cough, inability to speak, cyanosis or declining responsiveness indicate severe obstruction requiring action.
Responsive adult or child: alternate 5 back blows with 5 abdominal thrusts. This adds back blows to the older class sequence.
Late pregnancy or inability to encircle an adult abdomen: alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts.
Responsive infant: alternate 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts; never abdominal thrusts. The 2025 pediatric guidance uses the heel of one hand for infant chest thrusts.
If the patient becomes unresponsive, begin CPR with compressions and activate help. For witnessed choking collapse, do not delay for a pulse check.
When opening the airway for breaths, remove a visible object; never sweep blindly. Continue CPR/airway checks and follow the appropriate BLS algorithm.

objectives.objective: Discuss how to provide grief support for a patient’s family members and loved ones after resuscitation has ended.
objectives.summary: Support the family with clear information, privacy, and a calm presence during and after resuscitation.

sections.heading: During resuscitation
bullets: Designate one provider to communicate patient status while the team continues care.
Be concise, honest, and clear.
Recognize that emotional distress can become a medical crisis for a family member.

sections.heading: After unsuccessful resuscitation
bullets: Move family members to a quiet, private area when possible.
Introduce yourself and anyone with you.
Use the patient’s name and speak warmly and sensitively. The slides call for direct language, including the word dead, rather than confusing euphemisms.
Use eye contact and appropriate supportive touch.
Expect silence, crying, anger, or other emotional responses; do not insist on a particular reaction.
Be available without hovering. Ask whether a friend or relative can come to provide support.
Do not impose religious messages; respect the family’s beliefs.
Acknowledge children and provide age-appropriate support.
When leaving, turn support over to another appropriate person rather than abandoning the family.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: Family members may remember this event and how they were treated for the rest of their lives. Support at the beginning of grief can affect their ability to cope.

objectives.objective: Discuss the importance of frequent CPR training for EMTs, as well as public education programs that teach compression-only CPR.
objectives.summary: CPR competence requires repeated hands-on practice; public CPR and AED education helps care begin before EMS arrives.

sections.heading: Maintain EMT skills
paragraphs: CPR skills deteriorate over time. Frequent manikin practice maintains technique and helps providers coordinate compression, ventilation, switching, and AED tasks under pressure.
bullets: Practice hand placement, posture, complete recoil, controlled ventilations, and smooth role changes.
Use instructor-led training or video/computer-based self-instruction that includes hands-on practice.
Knowledge of the sequence alone is not equivalent to reliable physical performance.
Teamwork and quality review help identify and correct delays or poor technique.

sections.heading: Support public education
paragraphs: As a patient advocate, the EMT helps the community learn critical CPR and AED skills. Compression-only CPR education gives laypeople a way to start circulation support while emergency responders are on the way.
bullets: Facilitate training in CPR and AED use rather than assuming bystanders will already know what to do.
Consider teaching or assisting a community compression-only CPR course part of the professional responsibility described in this chapter.
Early bystander action strengthens the recognition, CPR, and defibrillation links in the chain of survival.
